#5672. Ask a Scientist: Who Has a Voice in Clean Air Protections?

If developers and planners decide to site an industrial chemical plant next door to your home, you’d want the chance to speak up about it. Soliciting input from the communities and individuals affected by pollution is an essential part of how environmental and public health laws are enforced. Under the federal Clean Air Act, large polluting facilities like power plants, chemical manufacturers, and refineries need to have a building permit, and every permitting decision must go through a “notice and comment” process. Although this is a federal law, it’s largely implemented by state, regional, and local agencies. And as a new UCS analysis shows, how much influence people have on the air permitting process varies greatly depending on where they live.

Darya Minovi leads fair access research for the Center for Science and Democracy at UCS. She is the lead author of Community Access to Clean Air Decisionmaking: Analysis of State Engagement in Title V Permitting, a new report that looks state-by-state at how people can make their voices heard.

AAS: What inspired you to do this analysis?

Darya Minovi: Last year, our team did an analysis of how the Trump administration is limiting public input on regulations andalso developed a set of recommendations for how government agencies should ensure the public gets to participate. With the administration very clearly side-stepping or ignoring these public processes, we did not, to put it lightly, expect the federal government to be a willing recipient of our research and guidance.

During the Biden administration, the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) did a lot of work to assess and expand meaningful public participation in government decisions. That was essentially all thrown away when President Trump was inaugurated. After consulting with colleagues and partners, we wanted to know: in this vacuum where the federal government isn’t interested in making progress, could we work with states to advance the public’s ability to participate in environmental policies?

AAS: Why does this participation matter, and how did you end up focusing on the air pollution permitting process?

DM: When you look at the core principles of environmental justice, meaningful engagement is central. People have the right to understand what’s happening in their communities and ideally be part of shaping those decisions. They need the opportunity to speak out and be respectfully listened to. People’s lived experience is expertise that can and should inform policy decisions. That’s democracy in action. At the federal level, environmental justice has been targeted and dismantled, but some states still value these

One specific environmental program where public participation is relevant is in Title V of the federal Clean Air Act (CAA), which covers operating permits for facilities that generate air pollution. This includes power plants, refineries, trash incinerators, and factories that manufacture chemicals—under the law, these are often called “major sources,” and there are very specific legal requirements about public participation. It’s one of the main ways air pollution gets regulated. But even though CAA is a federal law, it’s largely state and local agencies that carry out this permit process.

When a facility owner or company wants to apply for a permit to operate, they must submit a permit application to the relevant state, regional, or local agency. The agency writes a draft permit, which must be posted publicly in some way. The CAA requires agencies to accept public comments on the draft permit for at least 30 days and, if requested by the public, hold a hearing. Agencies also have a legal obligation to respond to substantive comments. These are very clear steps laid out in the law. It’s a high bar for participation, but we wanted to better understand how it works in practice.

What we found in our analysis is that the agencies with the authority to issue permits will approve Title V air permits unless there’s some clear problem with legal compliance. But the public can use that “notice and comment” process to slow down and influence what the facility will actually be permitted to do.

However, some agencies treat the public comment process as a set of boxes to check off. The law isn’t specific about meaningful engagement practices beyond public comment, so our analysis also looked at practices, programs, guidance, and laws at the state level, beyond what’s required by the federal government to enhance public participation in air permitting.

AAS: How did you do this analysis, and what did you find?

DM: We wanted to get the answers to three big questions.

We started with what I’ll call “desktop research”—reviewing agency websites and laws as though we were residents looking to navigate the process. All 50 states do have at least a website with some information. In general, agencies are posting draft permits and accepting public comments, as the CAA requires. But there are big differences in how that happens.

Public hearings aren’t very frequent and usually happen only if there’s a critical mass of people demanding them. We also reviewed nearly 90 permits from 35 different states—the public notices are often very technical, not easily readable by a layperson, and they’ll say things like “comments are due 30 days from posting date” instead of giving the actual dated deadline.

Very few states translate these notices into languages other than English. And we assessed whether the notices use “plain language” best practices—defining scientific terms, using white space and bullet points—and found that most states aren’t integrating these effectively. Minnesota and Michigan stand out as providing clear, readable information, and that’s largely the result of advocacy by local groups there.

We found that while 42 states had some resources describing how people can participate in permitting, the quality varied significantly. By and large permitting webpages and resources seem better designed for regulated industries, not the general public.

Ultimately, a public notice is only useful if you can find it, read it, and understand what it means and what you’re supposed to do to get involved!

We also wanted to know: do the comments make a difference? If they’re just going to get collected and sit on a shelf, that’s less meaningful than if agencies answer them or make actual changes to the permit in response. It’s very rare for agencies to deny a permit, but there are ways for public comments to have an impact—correcting errors, adding monitoring requirements, and strengthening enforcement.

AAS: You reached out to states to learn more. What did you find?

DM: Talking directly to these state agencies was an important part of our research. We built an 88-question survey, based on our September 2025 guidance, to ask agencies how they provide information, what they do to encourage participation, and what resources they have to carry the work out.

While we sent that survey to every state, only half the states responded in full, with 3 more responding partially. A few states said they intended to respond but didn’t, while others declined to participate or failed to respond entirely. That itself speaks to the capacity and, perhaps, interest these agencies have.

The states’ answers varied. Of the 28 states we heard back from, only 18 said they post responses to comments online, and only 13 could give us an example of when public comments resulted in a change to a permit.

At least 11 states have laws that go beyond what’s required in the CAA, and those laws often center environmental justice or cumulative impacts. States with these laws tended to have more readily available information on how to participate, as well as more resources and funding devoted to public outreach. Having these laws—or at least guidelines—in place does seem to create agency-wide changes to enhance public engagement.

Meaningful engagement takes time, money, and actual staff to manage the process. Only 20 of the agencies we spoke to provide training on public participation or environmental justice for staff, and only 16 have actual full-time staff dedicated to the process.

Unfortunately, the federal government is pushing in the opposite direction. Aaron Szabo, the (now former) director of the air-quality office at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, issued a memo urging states to expedite the Title V permitting process and rapidly review permits—saying explicitly that agencies don’t get many comments, so they don’t really matter.

DM: I was surprised by how much variability there was between and even within states. Some might have a lot of resources explaining how to participate in air permitting, but it’s a confusing website. Others might translate public notices in other languages but have no other information about how to participate.

While there’s a lot of room for improvement, there are some instructive examples too. For example, North Dakota has explicit guidance on how to write an effective public comment, with examples of common mistakes to avoid. Connecticut and Wisconsin have specific “how to” webpages to help people make comments or request a hearing. South Carolina has a webpage specifically entitled “Air Quality Decisions” that lays out what decision was made and posts the comments made in response to the draft permit. Ohio was the only state that got an “A” grade for readability of a public notice, with most states falling in the B/C range.

Every state can do better, of course, and we have a set of recommendations for how these agencies can improve. Governors, state lawmakers, and agency heads have a role to play here—certainly with funding for agencies and laws, but also in how they direct their agencies to carry this process out. Using public health data, translating notices into culturally appropriate languages and presenting them in plain language, making sure there’s fulltime staff devoted to public participation—these are just some of the steps to make participating in the air permitting process more meaningful, so that people not only have their voices heard, but actually have influence on decisions that shape air quality in their communities.

Courtesy of The Equation, UCS. By Seth D. Michaels.

#5671. How To Get A Screaming Deal On Your Next Car Rental

Whether you're flying with the family for a week of sun and sand with a whole lot of luggage and need transportation, or headed home for the holidays via I-94 and dread the overflow of humans and gifts and luggage all crammed into your daily driver, you may find yourself in need of a rental car.

But won't that be expensive? Perhaps not. We researched ways to save money on rental cars and interviewed two travel experts to get the inside scoop on keeping costs down. Victoria Fricke, owner of luxury travel agency Vic's Vacations, voted Indianapolis' Best Travel Agency, and Sharky Laguana, CEO of Bandago, which specializes in van rentals for bands and film crews, both lent their expertise. Laguana also chairs the board of the American Rental Car Association.

With our eye on reducing costs, ur recommendations include a range from planning ahead and shopping around to making deliberate decisions about insurance coverage when picking up the rental.

Laguana's recommends you book your car as soon as you know your travel dates. "If you book well in advance you can often find deals that don't exist days before pickup. The reason for this is straightforward. Car rental companies rely on early bookings to gauge demand, and having confirmed bookings in their back pocket allows them more room to experiment with higher prices as the date draws near."

Just be aware that if you do pre-pay, you may not be able to get a full refund if your plans change. For instance, Hertz will charge $100 if you cancel more than 24 hours prior to the reservation start date, and $200 if you're within 24 hours. Alamo is more generous, tagging you with a $50 fee for canceling before the 24-hour window and $100 within 24 hours of the loan start date.

As for weighing renting in town or at the airport, most of the time, according to reporting by NerdWallet, off-airport rental car reservations are cheaper. They looked at 20 different destinations and found that for rental car reservations lasting seven days, the average savings was $126 versus renting at the airport.

Still, it's a good idea to look at each location (city versus airport) and study the actual rates. You might also find a more limited selection of cars in cities than at the airport. And definitely read the fine print if you're thinking about a city pickup and airport drop-off, because that can add costly one-way fees.

Laguana explains that often, "Major online-travel aggregators (Expedia, Priceline, Kayak, etc.) have clauses in their agreements with car rental companies that prevent the rental companies from advertising rates lower than what the aggregators offer." Those deals don't necessarily cause higher prices for consumers. "Using a broker doesn't automatically mean you are paying more. But many companies, particularly the smaller independent companies, don't list their cars on aggregators." Fricke recommends online travel aggregators too, explaining, "I always start on Kayak. It's a great resource to pull all brands in comparison. I find this helps when searching for certain vehicle types like large sprinter vans. From there, I use that pricing once I've found my best-priced option, and I go direct." Meaning, after she finds the lowest price, she books directly through the car rental company.

While aggregators are a great place to start, you might miss a better deal if you only shop through those channels. Laguana explains, "Sometimes a simple Google search or chat with an AI agent will turn up rates significantly lower than what the aggregators have listed."

As for which rental car agencies are cheapest, NerdWallet's study of rental car companies found that Budget, Hertz, and Dollar consistently loaned cars for less. It's actually odd that there's any rate competition at all, since all of the major rental car brands are owned by just three companies.  Still, since you will be cross-shopping, know that Enterprise averaged $480 for seven days of rental, which was way cheaper than the $680 that National charged. Luckily, some of these players, such as Hertz, also have solid ratings and rent cool cars.

If you're a AAA member, you can save up to 20% off the base rate of all rental cars from Hertz, Dollar, and Thrifty. You can also add an extra driver for free. Costco pre-negotiates cheaper rates for its members and lets you add a second driver at no extra cost, which rental car agencies definitely charge more for.

Frequent-flyer programs also offer discounts on rental cars. For instance, United Airlines frequent flyers save up to 35% on base rates with Avis and Budget. USAA members (available to active duty military, veterans, and their families) can get up to 35% off current rental rates from Avis, Budget, Enterprise, Hertz, National, and Alamo rental agencies.‍ ‍

It's also possible your company or university alumni affiliation may offer discount codes. It's worth asking your employer or checking an alumni website to see if these exist – and you may have to present proof of the affiliation when you fetch the car. Also, make sure these codes aren't restricted to corporate travel rather than travel for pleasure, since violating those policies might endanger not just your affiliation but coverage during the rental.

"When I rent cars while traveling, I usually get most of the insurance products (although I will usually pass on the personal effects coverage)," Laguana says. "My reasoning: I'm driving in a location I'm not super familiar with, in a car I'm not super familiar with. Paying a little extra to avoid having to file a claim with my own insurance company makes sense to me." And for many, that peace of mind may well be worth the cost.

But if you have comprehensive car insurance, you might already have car rental coverage. You'll still be on the hook for your deductible, which you would be in an accident with your own car, too.

Also, check with your credit card company on their policies for car rentals. Often they bake in extra insurance coverage as long as you charge the car to them. For instance, the Chase Sapphire Reserve card adds $75,000 of damage coverage to the rental car. But that only applies to the car you're renting, not potential damage you might cause to another car or people outside the rental.

The key here is that the credit card saves you from taking out additional insurance from the car rental company. In fact, Chase's policy says you must decline the rental car agency's collision damage waiver or loss damage waiver (CDW and LDW) insurance so that Chase is your backstop. But, again, you'll still need your own car insurance supporting you in the event of an accident that causes other damage. This is often called supplemental liability protection, and you need to be certain your car insurance includes this. FYI, if you're traveling abroad, the rental company might say you have to buy that through them regardless.

Some rental car agencies offer a "mystery rental" option, meaning you don't get to choose the type or size of the car. "The mystery rental is usually a car that is not selling well," Laguana explains. "But it can still be a great deal, because the car rental company won't want to list that vehicle at such a low rate and have it find its way into various websites and search engines. So if you don't have specific needs and don't care what kind of car you get, this might be the best option."

As for other hacks and cautions, Laguana says renters can get into trouble by, "Not examining all the terms and conditions. Not long ago, comparing deals took a lot of work; now, AI makes it much easier. If you have a brand you trust, go with that brand. But if you don't know where to start, using AI can help you compare your options." That can help you avoid some of the most common rental car tourist scams.

Laguana goes further, explaining that there can be all sorts of hidden fees for non-vacation car rentals, too. "In our little sector, the passenger van rental business, we compete with businesses that have wildly different business models. Some offer cheap rates but then add required cleaning fees, additional driver fees, higher priced insurance products or lower mileage limits to make up the difference."

To avoid a scratch or ding getting chalked up to you during your rental period, Fricke advises clients "To ensure you take a video walking around the vehicle, checking for any damage (don't forget the inside). This ensures if there's any existing damage the rental car company doesn't place blame on you." If your inspection turns up damage that's not listed by the rental agency you need to call that out so they mark that down before you begin your loan.

Another good idea is to use an app like Gas Buddy so you know the price of gas near the rental agency. Most companies want to charge you their own per-gallon toll (usually higher than the going rate) if you bring the car back empty. Otherwise you need to fill it up before giving the car back. Maybe it's worth avoiding visiting a gas station before you return the car, but check the average gas price versus what they're charging so you're aware of the difference.

Finally, while you may want to rent someone's cool car through a peer-to-peer app like Turo, some policies, for instance getting coverage through your credit card, could be excluded. Chase explicitly excludes such rentals. Turo includes liability insurance in their loans (which covers third parties and their property), but says you should check with your car insurer to see if it covers peer-to-peer car loans — and cautions that most don't. For that reason they offer several tiers of insurance to cover damage to the loaned car. However, only their Premier tier prevents you from owing money for damages.

#5670. Secure Solar Futures set to install 313-kW array on Virginia elementary school

Secure Solar Futures, a commercial solar contractor, will build a 313-kW solar power system at Preston Park Elementary School in Roanoke, Virginia. Construction of the system is expected to start later this year at no cost to the Roanoke Schools through a 25-year power purchase agreement with Secure Solar Futures.

A total of 531 bifacial solar panels manufactured by VSUN Solar in Houston, Texas, will be installed on the rooftop of the school, and the array is expected to offset 67% of the power used by the school annually. In its first year, the school’s solar system is projected to produce 421 MWh of clean energy, enough to power 44 average Virginia homes.

Under the PPA, the solar power equipment will be provided at no upfront cost to Roanoke Schools. For the 25-year term of the agreement, Pardee Renewable Energy and Secure Solar Futures will own, operate and maintain the solar power system and will sell the energy produced to the school division at a rate lower than the local electric utility.

Preston Park Elementary School is expected to save $581,000 electricity costs over the term of the PPA. After the conclusion of the term, Roanoke Schools can opt to take ownership of the solar power system at a nominal cost, producing its own energy for the remainder of the equipment’s lifespan.

Billy Ludt is managing editor of Solar Power World and currently covers topics on mounting, inverters, installation and operations.

#5669. Advances and Unmet Needs in Pediatric Sickle Cell Disease

— It's better care that has led to better survival, not new treatment options

As the 1970s came to a close, sickle cell disease (SCD) remained largely a pediatric condition because few children born in the U.S. with the condition survived to adulthood. Today, about 95% of children born with SCD in developed nations survive to adulthood. Median life expectancy in the U.S. has reached 60 years, meaning half of all patients live to that age, as compared with less than 40% just 10 years ago.

The dramatic improvement in survival evolved from an amalgamation of factors including universal screening of newborns, prophylactic penicillin to prevent bacterial infections, immunization against Haemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pneumoniae, and broader and better-informed use of FDA-approved therapies for SCD. A recent multi-article review covered some of the key developments, as well as ongoing challenges and unmet needs.

Ironically, a clinical trial that did not meet its primary endpoint has profoundly influenced management of SCD. The randomized, placebo-controlled BABY HUG trial failed to show that hydroxyurea reduced the risk of kidney and spleen damage by 50% in very young children with SCD. Nonetheless, the trial showed that patients randomized to hydroxyurea had significantly fewer SCD-associated clinical events, including pain, dactylitis, acute chest syndrome, blood transfusion, and hospitalization. Investigators concluded that hydroxyurea "can now be considered for all very young children with sickle cell anemia."

BABY HUG was a landmark clinical trial because of the history of hydroxyurea, which was initially approved only for adults with SCD who met specific high-risk criteria. Published more than a decade ago, the trial established clinical principles that remain highly relevant today for children with SCD.

"[BABY HUG] gave us the evidence that hydroxyurea can be used as prevention, so before kids start having all these complications," Allison King, MD, MPH, PhD, of Washington University in St. Louis, told MedPage Today. "BABY HUG was really helpful because instead of being so reactive, the practice could be very proactive in pediatrics."

A recent analysis of more than 2,000 children with sickle cell anemia treated with hydroxyurea established long-term safety and efficacy. Children followed for as long as 8 years had significantly fewer and briefer hospitalizations, and laboratory data showed sustained improvement in hemoglobin in patients with good treatment adherence.

The Silent Cerebral Infarct Transfusion trial, published more than a decade ago, also had a transformative impact on SCD management. The results, in 200 children with sickle cell anemia, showed that regular blood transfusions significantly reduced the risk of silent cerebral infarction, which can have more subtle neurologic effects as compared with a stroke.

"A lot of our kids, and adults, have cognitive deficits, which are kind of like invisible disabilities because [the patients] can be quite verbal but have significant attention problems, processing speed, executive function that limit their ability to progress in their daily activities," said King. "Also, silent infarcts are a high risk for having overt strokes. Now it's an evidence-based guideline that we should be screening, as well as responding and transfusing, to prevent the progression."

Fast forward a decade and gene therapy became the next transformative clinical development in SCD, offering the potential for cure. Unfortunately, other therapeutic options for SCD have remained limited throughout the decade. One of the approved drugs, voxelotor (Oxbryta), was withdrawn from the market after post-approval data analysis and real-world clinical experience showed the benefits no longer outweighed the risks. Concern has arisen about the future status of another approved agent, crizanlizumab (Adakveo), which lost its conditional European marketing approval. Additionally, the drug failed to outperform placebo for reducing episodes of vaso-occlusive crisis in a recent phase III trial.

Moreover, cost and access remain major obstacles to expansion of gene therapy as a treatment option. In 2025, fewer than 200 patients worldwide received the two gene therapies, which come with a hefty price tag of $2-$3 million. Additionally, the process for screening and preparing patients for gene therapy can be "laborious" for many families, said King.

Despite the advances, more and more effective therapies are an ongoing need for patients with SCD, said Ofelia Alvarez, MD, of the University of Miami Health System.

"There is still a lot to do," she told MedPage Today. "The most widely used medication, hydroxyurea, does not work for all children with sickle cell anemia. Some patients do not respond. They continue to have low hemoglobin despite the treatment. We need new therapies to improve anemia, to decrease complications. They are always in need."

Better transitional care also has contributed to better survival in SCD. However, the quality of care and the ability to provide good transitional care vary greatly. Transition involves much more than handing off a patient from pediatric care to adult care, said Alvarez. Most young patients need to be educated about the disease itself, what medications are available and how they are used, and how to make appointments. Some need to learn about practical issues, such as budgeting, transportation, and learning to live independently.

"Here at the University of Miami, we have a very robust program that is co-created with patients and explained to the parents," said Alvarez. "After the transition, we follow up with the patients to see how they feel about the process and whether they have become integrated into the [adult] practice... . I personally don't have a lot of problems because I work very closely with the adult providers."

In some settings and circumstances, transition into adult care can be complicated and anything but a smooth process. The age at transition varies from practice to practice, but 18 is a common age. King, who specializes in caring for children, has expanded her patient age range up to 26. She described a 23-year-old patient whose circumstances are not rare in the SCD community.

"He has been intermittently homeless for 2 years," said King. "In his words, he 'couch surfs.' He doesn't have a stable place to live. He's not sure where he's getting his food. His meds are always being stolen, so he's frequently in the hospital for pain."

The case also illustrates the problem with using pain as a patient-reported endpoint for judging treatment efficacy, which has been a historical standard for the FDA.

"Pain is so multifactorial," said King. "It could be just sickling, and I'm not trying to minimize that, but it could be very biologically driven, but often, particularly in older teens and adults, psychosocial factors really are big drivers. That makes it difficult to tease out what's really driving a patient's pain."

Finding the origin of a patient's pain has been complicated by the fact that "for the last 20 years, we were sort of crawling our way out of the opioid crisis," said Jeffrey Glassberg, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City.

"When I was in med school, we were taught that there was no danger to opioids," Glassberg told MedPage Today. "If you're treating pain, no harm could come to the patient. Today, I think most people who treat a lot of sickle cell patients would agree: Opioids cause pain. Full stop."

"We have noted that the more opioids that we were giving over the last couple of decades, the more pain our patients would experience, and that pain is non-vaso-occlusive," he continued. "Our latest research is really finding that patients feel that the pain is identical to vaso-occlusive crisis ... The more opioids you give, the more pain that patients will experience that's non-vaso-occlusive, but feels the same."

A number of candidate drugs for SCD have failed to pass muster with the FDA because they did not show a reduction in vaso-occlusive crises. Moving away from that as an endpoint for efficacy and toward a more objective endpoint -- such as organ damage -- might increase the likelihood of more drug approvals and more treatment options for patients, said Glassberg.

#5668. Your Holiday Gifts Don’t Have To Be Delivered By Diesel

The 2026 holiday shopping season is soon to be upon us, with gift buyers and bargain hunters perusing stores in person and online. Behind the scenes, the US freight system has been working hard to transport the goods and gifts, traveling mostly by truck as they make their way through ports, warehouses, and highways.

So, what effect will the rising price of gasoline and diesel fuel have on the year’s biggest shopping season? The historic shock in prices at the pump has driven cost increases for the goods consumers buy throughout the economy, including holiday gifts, because costs to produce and ship goods have increased. Between January and October, the average national price for a gallon of diesel rose nearly 80 percent.

But it doesn’t have to be this way. The trucks moving and delivering goods throughout the economy don’t have to be subject to the high cost and volatility of the fossil fuel market. Globally, businesses are transitioning their fleets to zero-emission trucks. In addition to their public health and environmental benefits, zero-emission trucks (and battery-electric models in particular) offer significant reductions in operating costs compared to those powered by fossil fuels. This can help protect producers and consumers from expensive and volatile fuel prices and unhealthy air.

That can help us all breathe a bit easier.

This year’s holiday shopping season is marked by several unsettling trends—record high fuel prices and the second-largest monthly jump in the Producer Price Index (PPI) since 2010, as well as the largest 12-month increase in the PPI since 2022. This jump in the PPI, the measure of the costs incurred by US businesses to make, ship, and sell their goods, was meaningfully driven by the single largest month-to-month increase in producer energy costs in the past decade and a half. Additionally, September 2026 saw the third largest increase in transportation and warehousing costs under the PPI since 2010, only behind April 2026 and March 2022—the months following the beginning of the current US-Iran conflict and Russia’s war on Ukraine, respectively.

While Santa’s reindeer are primarily fueled by carrot snacks during the holiday season, according to the Alaska Department of Fish and Game, the rest of our nation’s freight system is most often powered by dirty and increasingly expensive fossil fuels. In September, diesel fuel prices hit record highs—topping as much as $9 per gallon at some retail gas stations. Diesel-fueled trucks are the workhorse of the US freight system, carrying more freight by weight than all other transportation modes combined. Each year, tractor trucks consume over 27 billion gallons of fuel, and fuel is the second-largest cost input to trucking after labor.

Higher fuel costs can ultimately be passed along to consumers and contribute to higher price variance for goods. This is particularly the case with certain food prices. A 2023 study in Energy Economics found that fuel price shocks accounted for nearly 20 percent of the price variance of cereals. Unfortunately, this means that even the reindeer aren’t immune to fossil fuel volatility.

Consumers may never see a fuel surcharge listed on a holiday gift, but fuel costs are embedded throughout the supply chain. When diesel prices spike, it becomes more expensive to move products between ports, warehouses, stores, and homes, even for carriers that hedge fuel prices through bulk or futures fuel agreements. Powering more of those trips with comparatively stable electricity can reduce one source of sudden cost pressure before products reach shopping carts.

Battery-electric trucks can provide far greater fuel cost predictability while also offering significantly lower per-mile fuel costs than fossil-fueled trucks. Between January 2016 and September 2026 (the most recent data month at the time of this publication), annual diesel price volatility averaged 3.75 times that of commercial electricity prices, according to our analysis of Federal Reserve and Energy Information Administration data. During this time, diesel prices saw a monthly spike of greater than 10 percent seven times, including four times in 2026. Diesel prices between February and March 2026 saw the highest price spike by far at over 32 percent. By contrast, the highest spike in the national average commercial electricity price in the last decade was 4.4 percent.

While it’s true that both diesel and electricity prices have increased this year, the magnitude of those increases is hardly comparable. Between January and September, the average national price for a gallon of diesel fuel rose nearly 80 percent compared to just two percent for average commercial electricity rates.

Consumers are paying for these higher petroleum prices at the pump and checkout lines, while oil companies and shareholders are seeing a windfall: both ExxonMobil’s and Chevron’s Q3 2026 earnings were more than double those of Q3 2025.

But the costs of our fossil fuel-powered freight system extend far beyond our wallets.

Fossil-fueled medium- and heavy-duty trucks are also the nation’s largest source of smog-forming pollution and account for the largest share of the nearly 10,000 premature deaths associated with transportation pollution in the US each year, despite making up just 13 percent of the vehicles on our roads.

Trucks are a particularly significant source of pollution in areas near the warehouses and logistics centers that our holiday packages travel through. For the 66 million people living near freight corridors, warehouses, ports, and railyards nationwide, the price of a fossil fuel-powered freight system is too often paid for with their health. Recent UCS research found that the 1.7 million people living near 10 or more freight facilities face a cancer risk from air toxics that is 32 percent higher than the national average.

While freight operators cannot control geopolitics and fuel prices, they can control which fuels they choose to use. Increasingly, freight operators are considering the switch to electric trucks, which offer more stable and affordable fueling costs with far less exposure to volatile global oil markets. FedEx, for example, recently announced plans to add 2,000 electric delivery trucks to its growing zero-emission delivery fleet.

The economics for zero-emission trucks are increasingly compelling—this is partially why we’ve seen continued adoption of electric commercial vehicles despite the current federal leadership’s best efforts to prolong our reliance on fossil fuels. Even states not typically thought of as electrification front-runners have seen meaningful growth in zero-emission delivery vehicles. In 2025, over 17 percent of new commercial vans in both Mississippi and Louisiana were zero-emission vehicles (ZEVs). In Georgia, nearly 35 percent of new commercial vans registered last year were electric.

California continues to lead the nation in overall deployments of zero-emission medium-and-heavy-duty vehicles, with zero-emission models accounting for over 24 percent of all new vehicle registrations in 2025. While this is a slight backstep from 2024 levels, California continues to see growth in the deployment of zero-emission tractor trucks. In California, ZEVs comprise around 8 percent of new tractor trucks registered in 2025, and it appears the momentum is just getting started. In the first three quarters of 2026 alone, California fleets applied for state clean truck incentives for more than 1,000 new electric tractor trucks—a clear example of growing interest and demand.

Momentum toward tractor truck electrification is picking up in other parts of the country as well. In September, Catalyst Mobility, a leading clean transportation nonprofit, announced that a group of major businesses, including Microsoft and Pepsi, placed a combined order for 2,500 battery-electric Tesla Semis—the largest single order of zero-emission trucks in US history. These trucks can travel up to 500 miles on a single charge at maximum legal capacity and regain 60 percent of range in a 30-minute charge. Earlier this year, Pilot Travel Centers announced a partnership with Tesla to install high-speed chargers for electric semi-trucks across major freight corridors in California, Georgia, Nevada, New Mexico, and Texas. The first of these stations is now operational.

Despite impressive momentum, private investments and market forces alone are unlikely to reliably electrify our freight system at the needed pace. The freight industry continues to face widespread adoption barriers, including higher upfront costs for many zero-emission truck models and lack of access to widespread, reliable commercial truck charging infrastructure. At the same time, consumers have limited ability to choose shippers committed to cleaner freight. We cannot simply toggle a “green delivery” option when shopping at a local store or online.

That’s where public policy comes in: to reduce barriers to electric truck adoption and accelerate the transition toward a cleaner, more affordable freight system.

At a time when the federal government’s support for freight sustainability and modernization has reversed and is undermining previous progress, state and local governments have the opportunity and responsibility to adopt and implement policies and programs that build momentum toward an electrified freight system. Specifically, they should accelerate zero-emission truck deployment where it is technically and economically feasible today, while addressing the technological and economic barriers that limit adoption elsewhere.

Policies and programs that drive electrification today while addressing barriers could include those that:

This holiday season, millions of gifts will move through a vast network of trucks, warehouses, and distribution centers before we give them to friends and loved ones. Increasingly, those trucks don’t have to run on diesel. Electric trucks offer a path toward a freight system that produces less pollution while reducing business and consumer exposure to the volatile global fossil fuel market.

However, widescale freight electrification is unlikely to occur at the pace needed without effective public policy. Smart public policies and programs can accelerate electric truck deployment where it already makes the most economic and environmental sense, while tackling the costs and infrastructure challenges that remain.

Consumers don’t always have the option or transparency to choose cleaner freight, but we can push our elected representatives to pursue policies and programs that deliver a more sustainable way to move the economy.

If you’re an early-career scientist, seasoned scientist, or technical expert, you can join our science network for opportunities to advocate for smarter transportation policies.

Courtesy of The Equation, UCS. By Sam Wilson.

#5667. If The Temerario's Exhaust Note Stopped You Buying One, Lamborghini Has Some Good News Made From Titanium

Despite the 10,000-rpm redline and its status as a mid-engined Italian supercar, the Lamborghini Temerario makes a noise that isn't universally loved. Our own Daniel Golson says this car's twin-turbo V8 is one of the best engines he's ever experienced, and Car Throttle says it sounds "incredible." Our own Andy Kalmowitz says it sounds "broken" below 3,000 rpm, while the Throttle House/Grand Tour guys once remarked that unless you're knocking on the redline's door, the Lambo simply "doesn't sound very good."

I think the Temerario having to live in the shadow of its naturally aspirated V10 Huracán predecessor has a lot to do with this mixed reception, but either way, Lamborghini has seemingly heard the feedback and is now raising the supercar's aural ceiling by offering a titanium exhaust from Akrapovič as a factory option. The upgrade is very much positioned as a sound enhancement, not necessarily a performance one, because in the first line of its press release, Lambo says it was "developed to amplify the natural acoustic character of its V8 engine while utilizing lightweight engineering."

These new optional pipes feature a different geometry and layout, physically wider tubes, custom manifolds, and a tailored silencer architecture. Strategic insulation keeps things cool in hot zones, and NVH was carefully calibrated so specific frequencies are enhanced. Lambo says this gives the Temerario "deep notes" at low rpm and an "incisive acoustic signature" at high ones.

It's made of high-grade titanium alloys, uses precision-cast valve housings, and is hand-assembled "across every component." Lamborghini says it weighs 25.1 pounds, 12% less than the standard exhaust, which means it cuts about 3.4 pounds from the car's curb weight. The tip is black to blend in with the car's rear end, and of course it says Akrapovič on the top so everyone at Cars & Coffee can know you spent the extra dough even when the car is off. There's good news for people who already have Temerarios looking for some extra, better decibels: the part will be available as a retrofit package.

We should note that, before this, the Temerario could already be had with a titanium muffler if you went for the lightweight Alleggerita Package that also bundled in a bunch of carbon-fiber bits, but this Akrapovič system is said to be new and therefore definitely not the same thing. Akrapovič is a Slovenian company that specializes in aftermarket exhausts, and has arguably become the name in the space, a bit like how Brembo is with brakes or Recaro is with seats. Lambo previously worked with Akrapovič on upgraded exhausts for the Urus SUV and Huracán STO.

For reference, the Temerario uses a twin-turbo 4.0-liter V8 along with three electric hybrid motors to produce 907 horsepower. For those who were on the fence about buying one because it apparently doesn't sound quite as nutty as that old V10 (I mean, that's why I haven't pulled the trigger yet), perhaps these new Slovenian pipes will change things for you.

#5666. 12 Of The Longest Range Electric SUVs In 2026

Just five years ago, cracking the 300-mile mark was seen as a major achievement for electric SUVs. Today, though, it's merely the norm, with even some affordable base models, like the Equinox EV LT1 and Mustang Mach-E Select RWD, easily surpassing that figure. Heck, newcomers like the BMW iX3 50 xDrive and Lucid Gravity Grand Touring offer more than 400 miles of range with dual-motor AWD and sports-car-like acceleration.

Crucially, the electric SUVs with the longest range in 2026 prove that the compromise era is over and that they are now a viable alternative to their gas counterparts. And it's not only because of the range. Most models we listed here also top up quickly, with some electric SUVs charging at up to 400 kW. As you'd expect from EVs, they are quick off the line, too.

For this list, we ranked the SUVs based on their EPA-estimated range, save for one EPA-exempt heavyweight. Also, all listed prices include destination charges. So, let's crunch the numbers and see how this year's electric SUVs compare.

The Equinox EV is quietly making a case as the smartest electric buy for 2027. After the out-of-control price drops for 2026, it now starts at an affordable $36,795. That's slightly less than the base Hyundai Ioniq 5 ($36,900) and only a bit more than the Toyota bZ ($36,575), but the Equinox EV beats both rivals handily when it comes to range.

Even the base single-motor FWD model (220 horsepower) comes with a fairly large 85-kWh battery, which provides a class-leading EPA-estimated range of 319 miles. Meanwhile, the base Ioniq 5 only packs a 63.0-kWh battery and a 168-hp motor, enough for a 245-mile range. The Toyota bZ has an even smaller 57.7-kWh battery that provides an even shorter 236-mile range and a less potent 165-hp front motor. Granted, the Equinox EV's 150-kW peak charging rate can't match the Ioniq 5's, but it keeps up with the Toyota bZ.

Better yet, adding a second motor has a negligible effect on range, with the AWD model rated at an EPA-estimated 307 miles between charges. Choosing the 300-hp AWD model does increase performance quite significantly, though. According to Car and Driver's tests, the FWD Equinox EV needs 7.7 seconds to reach 60, while the AWD cuts that down to 5.8 seconds.

The Equinox EV isn't only good at the numbers game. Inside, it offers enough room for adults in both rows and a useful 26.4-cubic-foot trunk. It also pampers passengers with a smooth ride, and it can even be equipped with GM's Super Cruise hands-free highway driving assistance tech.

The 2027 Kia EV6 ties the Equinox EV with an identical EPA-estimated 319-mile range. However, you'll need at least the Light Long Range trim, which starts at $42,745 and packs an 84-kWh battery alongside a 225-horsepower motor in the rear. The base 167-hp model has a smaller 63.0-kWh battery and an EPA-estimated range of only 237 miles, though it starts at a lower $39,445. Since it shares the 800-volt architecture with the Ioniq 5, the EV6 can use 350-kW chargers, which top up the larger battery from 10% to 80% in less than 18 minutes.

Although it looks like a futuristic hot hatch on the outside, the EV6 is a family car first and foremost. It has a spacious interior with ample room in both seating rows and a decent 24.4-cubic-foot trunk. Also, while the Equinox EV's hood packs only electronics, the EV6 has a small frunk for charging gear or a tire repair kit.

Kia's striking-looking EV also handles better than the Equinox EV, making it the preferred choice for enthusiast drivers. Still, getting the most out of the chassis requires opting for the 320-hp dual-motor variant, which sprints to 60 in 4.5 seconds as clocked by Car and Driver. Kia shelved the 641-hp GT variant in the U.S. this year — too bad, because it offered supercar-like pace (0 to 60 in 3.4 seconds), better handling, and virtual gear shifts.

The Mustang Mach-E is a veteran of the EV space, with the first model launched for the 2021 model year. Back then, the Mach-E had an EPA-estimated range of up to 305 miles with the extended-range pack (98.8 kWh gross, 88 kWh usable). The 2027 model can travel up to 320 miles with the same usable capacity, a clear sign of the improvements Ford made over the years.

For 2027, the Blue Oval discontinued the small 73-kWh battery pack, meaning the 88.0-kWh unit is standard across models except the performance-oriented GT and Rally trims, which come with an even larger 91.0-kWh pack. As part of the 2027 lineup overhaul, Ford also launched the Mustang Mach-E Trail package with a raised suspension, Michelin CrossClimate 2 all-season tires, and a 400W onboard inverter.

Now that the Mustang Mach-E comes with the extended-range battery as standard, it also starts a bit higher than its rivals at $42,040. Still, that gets you a fairly powerful 272-horsepower motor on the rear axle, which, according to MotorTrend, sprints to 60 in 5.7 seconds. The high-performance GT and Rally models are even quicker, both reaching 60 in just 3.3 seconds.

Because of its EV architecture, the Mustang Mach-E offers generous accommodations in both rows, alongside a good 29.7-cubic-foot trunk. It's a fairly comfortable and quiet cruiser, too, with Ford now offering the BlueCruise 1.5 hands-free driving tech on the base Mustang Mach-E Select trim to make long trips more relaxing for the driver.

With a base price of $65,895 and a 325-mile EPA-estimated range (with 19-inch wheels), the Audi Q6 e-tron seems overpriced next to its non-premium alternatives. Worse yet, opting for larger 20-inch rims drops the range to 301 miles.

Still, you do get more for your money here. Most notably, every Q6 and Q6 Sportback e-tron model comes with a 456-horsepower dual-motor AWD powertrain, which Audi says propels these SUVs to 60 in 4.9 seconds. Thanks to the advanced 800-volt architecture, Audi's electric SUVs also support quick charging at up to 270 kW. That's enough to charge the big 100-kWh battery from 10 to 80% in 21 minutes on supported chargers.

Befitting a premium SUV, the Q6 e-tron is very quiet and comfortable, especially when equipped with the optional air suspension. Furthermore, the cabin is roomy enough for adults, with the 30.2-cubic-foot trunk also ready to swallow larger cargo. The coupe-like Sportback model has a smaller 26.1-cubic-foot trunk because of the sloping roof, though.

Traditional Audi buyers might also find the interior a bit lacking in terms of luxury. Yes, the materials are nice, but most of the dashboard is covered with screens (the passenger screen is optional) and piano-black plastic, both of which are fingerprint magnets. Also, while Audi's buttons and switches still feel tactile and satisfying to use, most features are controlled via the infotainment screen. Luckily, Audi acknowledged this recently and plans to pivot back to better interior materials and more buttons.

Cadillac's rival to the Audi Q6 isn't equipped with dual-motor AWD as standard, but it's also cheaper at $61,195. The Lyriq is a significantly larger SUV, too, providing a comfortable seating space for up to five people. Its trunk isn't as big, though, offering only 28 cubic feet of hauling capacity. And while the Lyriq's cabin features a massive 33-inch curved OLED screen, it's also dressed up in different textures for a more luxurious vibe. In keeping with its luxury pedigree, the Lyriq is supremely quiet inside thanks to noise-canceling tech.

The base Lyriq packs one electric motor on the rear axle, but with 365 horsepower, it's at least potent enough for a brisk 0 to 60 time of 5.7 seconds, according to Car and Driver. With a 102-kWh battery onboard, this model can travel up to 326 miles on a charge per EPA estimates. The Lyriq can't match the Q6 e-tron at the plug, though, topping out at a modest 190 kW. According to Cadillac, a 10-minute charge at this speed adds 86 miles of range.

If you want more oomph, Cadillac offers a dual-motor AWD model with 515 hp, which cuts the range down to 319 miles. There is also the high-performance Lyriq-V for people who want it all, armed with 615 hp and a 3.0-second sprint to 60 in our testing, but also a shorter 285-mile range.

The Macan Electric started a new era for Porsche, one where existing internal-combustion nameplates are used for their all-electric counterparts. More than that, though, the Macan Electric is now one of the most advanced EVs on the market, packing an 800-volt architecture, a large 100-kWh battery, a 270-kW charging rate, active suspension, and active aero.

Appropriate for a Porsche, the Macan Electric also caters to enthusiast drivers with the GTS (563 horsepower) and Turbo Electric (630 hp) models. Still, those are expensive, starting at $107,650 and $115,050, respectively. If all you want is a premium electric SUV with a Porsche badge on it, the base Macan Electric starts at $82,650. Sure, it only packs a rear 355-hp motor, but it still gets to 60 in a respectable 5.4 seconds.

With an EPA-estimated range of 332 miles, the base RWD model gets the most out of the battery, too. With a 324-mile range, the 402-hp Macan 4 isn't too far behind, and offers the benefit of all-wheel drive. The even peppier Macan 4S packs 509 hp, though it has a significantly shorter 290-mile range. (The GTS and Turbo models offer 294 and 293 miles of EPA-estimated range, respectively.)

Where the Macan differs from other electric SUVs is the driving experience, as it combines a poised, neutral chassis with communicative steering. It rides well, too, particularly the base model, which combines the standard air suspension with smaller 20-inch wheels. Unfortunately, the Macan Electric isn't very accommodating in the rear and has a tight overall cargo capacity of 22.1 cubic feet.

The aero-focused Hyundai Ioniq 9 makes you think twice about getting a premium five-seat SUV. Starting at around $61,000, it offers generous space in the first two rows and adds a useful third row for kids. Sliding the second-row seats reveals even more kneeroom at the back, with a useful 22-cubic-foot trunk behind the third row. Fold the third row flat, and the cargo capacity grows to 46 cubic feet, far surpassing that of five-seat electric SUVs.

The practical interior isn't the Ioniq 9's only strength. Its large 110.3-kWh battery gives the base rear-wheel-drive model an excellent 335 miles of range, while the 800-volt architecture lets it use 350-kW chargers. Yes, it only has 215 horsepower and needs 7.8 seconds to reach 60 (as tested by MotorTrend), but that's still quicker than the 2027 Palisade V6, which packs 287 hp and sprints to 60 in 7.9 seconds.

Both of the Ioniq 9's dual-motor versions also provide a 300-plus-mile range. The 303-hp Long Range model can travel 320 miles before the battery is depleted, while the 422-hp Performance model cuts that figure by only nine miles. The Ioniq 9 Performance is also genuinely quick in a straight line, ripping to 60 in 4.4 seconds.

The 2027 Tesla Model Y Premium RWD packs a relatively small 81.0-kWh battery, yet it can travel 355 miles with a full battery per EPA estimates. It does that by being very efficient with its use of electricity, meaning you'll spend less out of pocket per mile than in other EVs. The Model Y can also charge at a rate of up to 250 kW, restoring 182 miles of range in just 15 minutes.

The $47,630 Model Y Premium comes with a rear 304-horsepower motor as standard, which offers a brisk 0 to 60 time of 5.1 seconds, per Car and Driver. For $4,000 extra, you can add another motor on the front axle, which bumps the output to 397 hp and cuts the 0 to 60 sprint to 3.9 seconds and the EPA-estimated range to 327 miles. The base Model Y, which starts at $41,630, has a smaller battery and a 295-hp rear motor, but still extracts a good 321 miles on a charge.

The Model Y is fairly spacious inside and can carry 29.5 cubic feet of cargo. Buyers who want more room can now opt for the 7.0-inch-longer Model Y L, which adds a third row in the rear to accommodate up to six passengers. With the third row folded, it boasts a sizeable 38-cubic-foot trunk. Sold strictly in Premium trim, the Model Y L commands $63,630 for 332 miles of range.

With a base price of $85,885, the Rivian R1S is a significant step up from the Ioniq 9. Like its Hyundai rival, Rivian's SUV has three seating rows, with enough space for adults in the first two rows, but only for kids at the back. Luggage space behind the third row is on the snug side at 18 cubic feet (expanding to 49 folded), though a generous 10-cubic-foot frunk helps the R1S narrow the gap.

Where the R1S differs from its competition, however, is its off-road focus. Even the base model comes with a 533-horsepower dual-motor AWD powertrain and multiple drive modes that make the most out of it on slippery terrain. It's quick, too, dispatching 0 to 60 in 4.5 seconds. When equipped with the standard battery, the R1S has a 329-mile range, though the Long Range pack bumps this to 410 miles for $7,000.

The model range gets crazier as you go up the ladder; the R1S is also available in a 665-hp dual-motor guise, an 850-hp tri-motor beast that sprints to 60 in 2.9 seconds, and an unhinged quad-motor variant with 1,025 hp and a supercar-like 0 to 60 time of 2.6 seconds. Crucially, the Quad's four independent motors deliver precise, wheel-by-wheel torque control to maximize off-road traction.

Based on the Neue Klasse platform, the iX3 represents BMW's most consequential foray into the EV space, and the spec sheet immediately backs it up. Most notably, the massive 112-kWh battery pack, currently the only one available in the U.S., provides a class-leading 434-mile EPA-estimated range when equipped with 20-inch wheels and summer tires. The battery can also be topped up at a class-leading 400 kW, adding a whopping 230 miles of range in about 10 minutes. As a cherry on top, the iX3 50 xDrive comes as standard with a 463-hp dual-motor powertrain that allows a brisk 4.7-second 0 to 60 time.

But the Neue Klasse platform also brought some controversial changes. The iX3's interior is now almost fully digital, packing a 17.9-inch touchscreen that includes all climate controls and a 43.0-inch panoramic display under the windscreen. The steering wheel houses most of the buttons, but it's an awkward squircle shape that requires an acclimation period. Fortunately, despite being made mostly of sustainable materials, the iX3's interior feels premium. It's spacious for passengers, too, with a 30-cubic-foot trunk and a 2-cubic-foot frunk providing decent cargo storage.

The Lucid Gravity blurs the line between a minivan and an SUV, and we don't mean it in a bad way. It has by far the most practical cabin of all three-row electric SUVs, with ample space for adults in each row, multiple storage areas, and a large 48-cubic-foot trunk if you fold the third row. Keeping all seats in place leaves a smaller 15-cubic-foot cargo volume, but there is an additional 8-cubic-foot front trunk. The dashboard is unfortunately an all-digital affair, with a massive 34-inch curved display and a 12.6-inch touchscreen, but at least they are nicely integrated into the dash.

The brilliance of the Lucid Gravity goes beyond the practical interior. Based on an advanced 926-volt architecture, the Gravity supports charging speeds of up to 400 kW. It's efficient, too. The base $81,750 Gravity Touring model has a relatively small 89-kWh battery, yet it's still rated at 337 miles of range — impressive considering it has a dual-motor 560-horsepower drivetrain.

The $100,750 Gravity Grand Touring adds a larger battery for an EPA-estimated range of up to 450 miles. It also packs more oomph at 828 hp, enough for a blazing 0 to 60 sprint of 3.4 seconds. Lucid also offers a high-performance GT-S model with 1,070 hp that reaches 60 in just 3.1 seconds, but it also costs a steep $127,750.

The Cadillac Escalade IQ is all about big numbers. At a colossal 9,120 pounds, the Escalade IQ Luxury is heavy enough to escape the EPA's jurisdiction for official range testing. Still, according to Cadillac's estimates, the electric SUV behemoth can travel 465 miles before the battery depletes. Hardly surprising, as it comes with a gargantuan 205-kWh battery, enough for three compact SUVs with a ~250-mile range. Thanks to the 800-volt architecture, the Escalade IQ supports 350-kW DC charging.

Although it weighs significantly more than a fully equipped AWD pickup truck, the Escalade IQ is quick off the line, reaching 60 mph in a brisk 4.7 seconds. That's impressive considering the heft the 750-horsepower dual-motor AWD powertrain needs to deal with, but short of the 682-hp Escalade-V's 4.4-second sprint. Still, the Escalade IQ is significantly cheaper, with the base Luxury trim starting at $132,695, while the Escalade-V costs $172,195.

Now, sure, you don't get the sound from the Escalade-V's 6.2-liter supercharged V8 in the IQ, but if luxury is what you are after, the electric model delivers. Inside, the Escalade IQ treats occupants to palatial proportions across the first two rows, though you need the long-wheelbase IQL for an adult-friendly third row. Like the gas-powered Escalade, the IQ has a tech-forward interior with a massive 55-inch dashboard display, which is easy to use but offers no smartphone mirroring.

#5665. Hydropower Generation in the Southwest Fell to Record Lows This Summer

Prolonged drought conditions affecting the Colorado River Basin led to record low hydropower generation this summer in the Southwestern electricity supply region, which includes Arizona, New Mexico, and small parts of Nevada and California. Hydropower generation from April through August 2026 was 19% lower than during the same period last year and 28% lower than the 10-year average, according to the latest data from our Form EIA-923 survey.

Water elevations at Lake Powell and Lake Mead, which are formed by the Glen Canyon Dam and Hoover Dam, respectively, hit record lows. To be able to generate hydropower at the Glen Canyon Dam, Lake Powell should have an elevation of at least 3,490 feet, also known as the minimum power pool. At the end of September, this elevation reached 3,518 feet, less than 1% above minimum power pool. The Hoover Dam requires an elevation of at least 950 feet at Lake Mead, which by the end of September reached 1,038 feet, 9% higher than minimum power pool. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation manages most dams across the Colorado River Basin. Seven states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) depend on the river for hydropower generation and for other water supply needs. To mitigate the risk of Lake Powell’s water elevation falling below the minimum power pool, water was released from Flaming Gorge, a reservoir located in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Additionally, water releases from Lake Powell were reduced to maintain an elevation of at least 3,510 feet given the most probable water inflows.

However, lower water releases from Lake Powell could also impact water elevation downstream at Lake Mead, in turn affecting hydropower generation at the Hoover Dam. To address this possibility, the Department of the Interior decided to reduce the collective water consumption of California, Arizona, and Nevada by 1.25 million acre-feet each year over the next two years.

We expect hydropower generation in the Southwest will total 6.13 billion kilowatthours (BkWh) in 2026 in our November Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), 9% lower than last year and 24% lower than the 10-year average. In 2027, we expect hydropower generation in the Southwest to total 6.1 BkWh, 0.5% lower than this year. This year’s El Niño could bring more precipitation than normal, providing some drought relief and improving the hydropower generation forecast in the region. However, one good water year likely won’t eliminate the effects of multiple years of water scarcity.

According to the STEO, hydropower generation in the Southwest is expected to account for about 4% of the region’s generation mix in 2026. That share has declined from a peak of 8% in 2011.

Article from Today in Energy. Principal contributor: Lindsay Aramayo.

The EIA collects, analyzes, and disseminates independent and impartial energy information to promote sound policymaking, efficient markets, and public understanding of energy and its interaction with the economy and the environment.

#5664. SOLRITE and sonnen collaborate on integrated VPP breaker

SOLRITE and sonnen plan to digitally integrate VPP smart breakers into what the companies are calling the SOLRITE sonnen VPP. The expanded VPP Node combines sonnenHub with ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart breaker technology to manage major household loads. The VPP smart breaker, controlled by ADAPT Energy, can also participate in on-grid VPP events, enabling the same electrical infrastructure to be used for both backup and grid participation.

“Our work with ADAPT Energy is a meaningful step forward in how we think about residential battery storage and VPP participation,” said Regan George, CEO and founder of SOLRITE Energy. “We have already demonstrated the tremendous value of connecting sonnen batteries together as a pooled grid asset. Now, we’re going inside the home and unlocking another layer of flexibility that has been sitting there all along. By combining the battery with additional load management made possible by the VPP smart breaker technology, we’re creating a more valuable node for the grid while also giving homeowners a clever backup solution.”

The system can shed large loads without requiring those circuits to be relocated. ADAPT Energy keeps the smart breakers synchronized with the sonnen battery during backup mode and automatically restores the breakers when grid power returns.

This integration is designed to manage whole-home electrical loads in the background, not requiring homeowners to reset circuits during an outage.

“This is about making whole-home backup work the way homeowners expect it to,” said Troy Morgan, president of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy. “Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired, and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home. Our technology empowers home loads to supply optimal backup power during an outage or provide valuable flexibility to the grid.”

When a VPP event happens, the sonnen battery can discharge or charge with direct load shedding via ADAPT. ADAPT Energy will strictly shed pre-approved household loads. A customer who has opted to include a pool pump, for example, can have that load temporarily turned off while the sonnen battery is discharging to the grid.

“With the addition of ADAPT Energy’s VPP smart-breaker technology to the SOLRITE–sonnen ecosystem, we are expanding the virtual power plant from a battery-centered resource into a fully orchestrated home-energy platform,” said Blake Richetta, chairman and CEO of sonnen. “By synchronizing energy that has been harnessed in our battery with intelligent, real-time control of household electrical loads, we can deliver more flexible, responsive capacity to the grid precisely when it is needed most. This integration materially strengthens the value of SOLRITE’s virtual power plant—supporting grid reliability, creating greater customer value, and enabling SOLRITE to continue delivering industry-leading solar-plus-storage VPA solutions to homeowners.”

Billy Ludt is managing editor of Solar Power World and currently covers topics on mounting, inverters, installation and operations.

#5663. This Tractor Supply Mini-Excavator May Not Be The Smallest, But It Is One Of The Cutest

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Remember playing with your Tonka trucks as a wee kiddo? If you grew up before tablets displaced little metal keepsakes, you ruled an imaginary work site, moving clumps of sand, dirt, and mud from one place to other spots. Granted, those other places were often your hair, shirt, and pants pockets. Oh, those were the days. Fret not, forever child — Yardmax has a tool that bridges the gap between practical equipment and a rideable Tonka-style toy.

It's the Yardmax YE0610, a 1,432-pound mini-excavator with a host of available attachments, from a claw to a grading bucket and rake.  Better yet, you might just be able to scoot on down to your local Tractor Supply and pick one up.

That said, Yardmax's diminutive earth mover isn't the smallest thing in the mini-excavator market. In fact, if you want to get crazy with your tiny tools, Honda and Komatsu once teamed up to make what may very well be the cutest little digging machine ever.

You've seen the big stuff. You know, the massive, earth-moving heavy construction equipment required to build a modern highway. Monstrous bulldozers, cold milling machines, and long-necked dinosaur-ish excavators are all part of the process. Some of these dirt-munching excavators can get properly huge, with the biggest examples tipping the scales at over 2 million pounds. Yes, you read that right.

Other excavators, however, go for more of a park-it-in-your-garage footprint. That's what the Yardmax YE0610 mini-excavator is all about. At just 27.5 inches wide, the wee digging machine's width takes up considerably less floor space than a common go-kart. Even with the canopy installed on the YE0610-575003 model, the mini-excavator is 62.4 inches tall and 1,674 pounds. Opt for the topless base YE0610, and that weight drops to 1,432 pounds. Not exactly a 2-million-pound earth mover.

Okay, so it's cute. Can it dig? Yardmax asserts the YE0610 can dig up to 47.2 inches deep, or just under four feet. Then there are the attachments. Depending on the model, the Yardmax can use a claw, grading bucket, or rake for your digging, filling, clearing, and leveling tasks. As far as power goes, the mini-excavator features a 306-cc engine capable of hustling the little machine at a cautious 1-mph pace. As expected, the excavator can rotate 360 degrees, regardless of track position.

This wee workhorse might be one of the wildest things Tractor Supply sells. Then again, it might not be. After all, this is a retailer that also offers a teeny tiny minibike to awaken your inner child.

As of this writing, the Yardmax YE0610, complete with its removable canopy, grading bucket, and rake, is for sale at Tractor Supply for $6,999.99. Want to save a couple hundred bucks on your backyard digging machine? The same setup is available at Walmart for $6,799. Of course, if you'd rather go in another direction entirely, Tractor Supply also sells a Power Wheels-esque mini truck. Your mini truck won't likely do any excavating for you, though.

Here's the thing, though: the Yardmax YE0610 isn't the smallest thing on the mini-excavator market. Croba, a sub-brand of MechMaxx, produces a MEC06 mini-excavator that weighs 87 pounds less than the Yardmax and undercuts the Tractor Supply price for the YE0610 by nearly $2,000, though its max digging depth falls shy of the YE0610 by 3.9 inches.

Like a shrinking set of nesting dolls, things can get even smaller. Komatsu, a Japanese heavy machinery manufacturer, joined forces with Honda in 2022 to produce an unbearably cute rideable excavator for the Japanese market. The result was the Komatsu PC01E-1, a 750-pound electric micro excavator with unmistakable toy aisle looks.

Better yet, the PC01E-1 falls just shy of the 771.6-pound max load capacity of Japanese mini trucks. So, go ahead, load your pint-sized electric excavator into your tiny truck.

#5662. 10 Reasons for the Big Blue Wave

I wrote the other day about a top reason US voters said they voted for Democrats in such large numbers — corruption in the Trump household, Trump administration, and Republican Party. It was surprising to me that this showed up as the biggest factor for so many people … even though it was also a huge one for me. However, I think everyone knows what the most significant reason was for the dramatic, historic shift in voting. It’s the economy, stupid! That’s the famous old quote from James Carville, a political strategist working for Bill Clinton when he was running for president in 1992, and it’s as relevant as ever. With that in mind, let’s take a look at some of the top reasons for the Big Blue Wave.

Inflation has hit and hit and hit. Donald Trump said while campaigning for president in 2024, “Starting on day one, we will end inflation and make America affordable again.” However, of course, beyond the fact that he didn’t come close to doing that and was just making an obviously false promise, Trump actually jacked up inflation significantly with his obsessive, high tariffs and with his war on Iran. Whereas it’s often hard to tie inflation to a specific presidential policy, in this case, we had two specific presidential policies that clearly caused inflation! Even when there are no clear links, voters blame the president for such matters, so imagine how much they must have done so in this case!

Aside from inflation, the economy overall isn’t great. The country isn’t adding a bunch of jobs, wages and salaries aren’t rising much, and people by and large don’t feel optimistic about their financial futures. So, combined with quickly rising costs, a very meh economy had voters wanting change.

As already discussed at length, voters were fed up with corruption in the Republican Party. As some CleanTechnica readers pointed out, if people were prospering financially and not being hit with severe inflation, many of them probably wouldn’t care about the corruption. However, when considering #1 and #2, people naturally get quite frustrated with blatant corruption and essentially high-volume robbery from Donald Trump, the Trump family, Trump staffers, and the Republican Party broadly.

Naturally, this is heavily linked to #1, since it is largely this war that has led to gas prices rising so much. However, also more broadly, Americans are fed up with forever wars in the Middle East, there’s never been a good and strong case for why Trump started this war (as tends to be the case with these wars in the Middle East), and many people really don’t like seeing innocent schoolchildren being bombed to death. Trump was supposed to be an anti-war president (I know that many people believed that, even though Trump is a naturally aggressive, violent person who seemed to me like someone who would obviously get into wars). Voters who cared a lot about this topic might have felt betrayed by Trump and swung strongly away from him and the Republican Party (which has a tendency to get us into these oil wars in the Middle East).

Even for many people who thought we needed stronger actions to stop people from coming to the United States, the inhumane, deadly, Gestapo-like ICE army — often including violent people with their faces covered and without ID acting like the mafia — was a step or ten too far. There are countless stories of good, innocent people being jailed without cause, or even murdered, by this Nazi-like police force. There was clearly a huge blue shift in certain places as a result of this.

Many voters have gotten extremely concerned about Republicans under Trump’s leadership eroding the foundations of our democracy. While this became a major problem in Trump’s first term, he has gone much further in his second term. Apparently, more people have woken up to this problem and it has freaked them out.

A massive rollout of AI and data centers — often feeling completely forced on us — has upset a lot of Americans. This does come back to #1, too. Giant data centers have jacked up electricity prices a ton in several regions. Others are threatened with the same thing happening. The same thing has also happened from the crypto craze, which more and more people have also found to be a scam. Seeing billions upon billions trillions of dollars funneled toward AI companies while people are struggling, and then seeing electricity prices rising significantly — surprise, surprise — pisses people off and makes them vote for change.

No matter how you cut it, people vote based on money — in particular, their own money. Whether it’s food prices, gas prices, electricity prices, clothing prices, doll prices, computer prices, car prices, or other prices, people don’t like it when they have to pay a lot more money for stuff — especially when they aren’t making much more money, or more money at all. Simply put, this matter deserves extra weight, because the critical thing swing voters are often voting on is just that — money.

Of course, there are solar, wind, and EV aspects to all of this. Trump has made the US spend a fortune to stop wind and solar farms from providing the US with cheap electricity, and he has made the US spend a fortune keeping old, dirty coal power plants open. High gas prices have also pushed people to buy electric cars, but mostly in other countries where there’s more EV choice and more people have more sense on this topic. However, by and large, I don’t think American voters really shifted much based on Trump stopping renewable energy projects, promoting coal and gas, or limiting EV choice in the United States. People voting for Democrats on climate and cleantech matters were already voting for Democrats based on these issues. It’s unlikely many people at all shifted from red to blue because of these factors.
