#5661. Response to Standard PBC Treatment at 1 Year Linked to Lower Long-Term Risks

— "Response predicts outcomes in real-world care, and nonresponders carry a risk," researcher says

A biochemical response to ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) at 12 months was associated with lower 5-year risks of hepatic decompensation and mortality in patients with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), a propensity-matched landmark cohort study suggested.

Among patients considered to be responders -- defined as an alkaline phosphatase (ALP) level ≤130 U/L and a bilirubin level ≤1.0 mg/dL -- the 5-year cumulative incidence of hepatic decompensation was 10.2% versus 17.8% among nonresponders (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.51-0.70, P<0.001), reported EzzElDien A. Ibrahim, MD, MSc, of the University of Missouri in Columbia, at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases annual meeting in Denver.

In addition, the cumulative incidence of 5-year all-cause mortality was 12.2% among responders versus 16.3% for nonresponders (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65-0.84, P<0.001).

Other clinical outcomes also trended in favor of or significantly favored responders:

"Response predicts outcomes in real-world care, and nonresponders carry a risk," Ibrahim said. "We can check ALP and bilirubin at 1 year on UDCA," and at that point, clinicians should consider "escalating nonresponders without delay."

UDCA is the first-line treatment for PBC, a rare and chronic autoimmune disease of the bile ducts, "and it ... works," Ibrahim noted.

An international cohort study that included 3,902 patients from the Global PBC Study Group database showed that after inverse probability treatment weighting, the 10-year cumulative liver transplant-free survival rate was 79.7% among UDCA-treated patients and 60.7% among untreated patients, with UDCA treatment resulting in a statistically significantly reduced risk of liver transplant or death (HR 0.46, 95% CI 0.40-0.52, P<0.001).

However, 20% to 40% of patients do not respond biochemically to UDCA at 12 months. In 2024, seladelpar (Livdelzi) and elafibranor (Iqirvo) were granted accelerated approval for patients with PBC who either did not respond to UDCA or were intolerant to the treatment.

While a number of criteria such as the PARIS criteria link 12-month response to UDCA to outcomes, Ibrahim said real-world validation in routine care for 5-year clinical endpoints -- such as decompensation and death -- is limited.

This explains "why this study matters," he noted.

For this study, Ibrahim and colleagues used the TriNetX U.S. Research Network that includes data on 147.5 million patients from 112 health systems.

They included matched cohorts of 2,911 patients with PBC. Mean age was 61.3, 87% were women, 77% were white, 34% had a cirrhosis code, 14% had portal hypertension, and mean albumin level was 3.86-3.91 g/dL.

Responders and nonresponders to UDCA were categorized based on propensity score matching of 29 covariates that included demographics, liver and mental health comorbidities, alanine aminotransferase levels, aspartate aminotransferase levels, platelet counts, albumin levels, and international normalized ratio.

Ibrahim acknowledged that the study had a number of limitations, including the fact that PBC was defined by codes and not by a positive anti-mitochondrial antibody test or histology. In addition, there was no access to UDCA dose or adherence data, and there were a limited number of 5-year events for the liver transplant and hepatocellular carcinoma analyses.

#5660. Was The Tesla Roadster Reveal Realistic? Engineering Explained Fact Checked It

Unless you've been living under a rock, it's unlikely that you've missed Tesla's wild Roadster event, or at least haven't heard about it. In all honesty, the reveal (or rather re-reveal) was actually pretty insane. While the upside-down stunt was already accomplished by the McMurtry Spéirling, the rest of the show (regardless of whether you're a fan of Elon) left enthusiasts in genuine awe. The car flew, did a kickflip, and even managed a crazy 0-60 time (without rollout) of 0.81 seconds.

If only there was someone with a whiteboard who could break down the physics and legitimacy of the new Roadster and its many engineering feats. That's precisely what Jason Fenske from YouTube's Engineering Explained set out to do. Because specifications of the Roadster aren't available yet, including weight distribution, dimensions, and so on, Fenske had to improvise with assumptions. But the gist is: the new Tesla Roadster reveal appears to be legit, though with a few caveats.

Fenske begins by analyzing the Roadster's fan-assisted aerodynamics. For the Roadster to stay upside down (as seen in the demo), the estimated pressure differential is around 11.5 kilopascals (kPa), — an 11.5% vaccum — achieved with help from fans that suck air out of a small area underneath the car that's sealed using deployable skirts.

That 11.5 kPa is the pressure difference between the top of the car (1 atmosphere, or approximately 100 kPa) and the bottom of the car (88.5 kPa), arrived at using the downforce figures from Tesla's demo and Fenske's assumption of the Roadster's skirt area. While he reckons the system could theoretically generate up to 90,000 kilograms of downforce (if that 88.5 kPa is brought down to zero, i.e., 100% vacuum), the car only needed an 11.5% vacuum to stay upside down.

Next up, Fenske breaks down the Roadster's brief flight and kickflip demonstration. For that, the mass flow rate of the 250 kilograms of available nitrogen (stored at 10,000 pounds per square inch in the two storage tanks) is determined using rocket science and a few assumptions. Dividing the available mass of nitrogen (250 kilos) by the mass flow rate (37 kg/s) reveals that the Roadster (in Rocket spec) can hover in the air for about seven seconds. Fenske reckons that both stunts are possible, considering each took around four seconds to complete. Whether Tesla used larger storage tanks or a lighter shell is debatable, but the demo appears to be plausible.

As for the 0-60 times, Fenske starts with the Base Roadster, which is yet to be confirmed as a production model. In any case, plugging the variables (most of which are assumptions) into a fancy equation reveals that the Base Roadster can achieve a maximum acceleration of 0.99 g. This translates to a 0-60 time of around 2.76 seconds. On the Performance variant, which comes equipped with the fans, Fenske arrives at an estimated 2.3 g and 1.2 seconds for its 0-60. However, he does mention caveats, as variables like the friction coefficient and pressure distribution can influence the final number.

To see whether the Thrust version can actually run a 0-60 of 0.81 seconds, he connects the model's acceleration of 3.37 g to the mass flow rate of nitrogen (37 kg/s). According to Fenske, if you only need around 40 kilos of nitrogen to deliver 1 g for 1.0 seconds, the 200-liter storage tank has enough and more to hit 3.37 g. As for the Rocket variant, Fenske estimates a 0-60 time of 0.5 seconds, pulling a whopping 5.5 g based on his assumptions.

At the end of the day, this event was a great marketing stunt. And that's pretty much how Fenske sees it, because the Roadster's upside-down trick has a few real-world nuances to consider. For instance, the skirts are a wear item, as are the fans. Using the McMurtry as an example, he explains that debris can still enter the fans no matter how efficiently the system filters out the air. Also, the downforce levels depend on the surface, and the demo uses an ideal setup, according to Fenske, which is far from the typical unevenness of actual road surfaces. So real-world performance may be different.

Perhaps the bigger question is: Will this Roadster ever end up in the hands of a consumer? After all, we have seen many of Musk's promises never materialize. There was the promise of a 500-mile Cybertruck and Model S. Those never happened, and neither did many of the previous Roadster's claims. That car was supposed to have four seats and a 620-mile range. The new one is a two-seater (or single-seater, depending on the model), and Tesla's VP of vehicle engineering, Lars Moravy, told Top Gear it will end up with only around 310 to 320 miles of real-world range. Heck, the new car isn't even really a roadster — it's a T-top.

Musk claims the production Roadster will do even better than what was shown in the event, and Tesla says it will enter production in 2028. But as Fenske points out in the video, "Tesla says things and then they do not do those things ... You really don't know with this company until the product actually ships." So let's leave it at that.

#5659. Comparative Cost Analysis for Residential Curbside Organics Collection Programs

This analysis of eight residential programs shows that, if properly implemented, cities can use a new organics collection program to build a more efficient, resilient, and sustainable solid waste system.

Residential curbside organics collection is expanding across the United States as states and local governments seek to reduce food waste sent to landfills and incinerators, meet waste diversion and climate goals, and respond to landfill capacity constraints. Yet for many communities, the perceived cost of adding organics recycling collection atop existing trash and recycling collection remains a significant barrier to implementation.

NRDC’s Comparative Cost Analysis for Residential Curbside Organics Collection Programs report finds that there is no single predetermined cost of implementing and operating an organics collection program. The cost to communities depends substantially on how organics collection is designed and, critically, how it is integrated into the broader solid waste system. A municipality that simply adds weekly organics collection to an otherwise unchanged garbage and recycling program is likely to see an increase in cost. However, a municipality that uses the introduction of organics to evaluate and optimize collection frequency, routes, contracts, processing arrangements, participation, and funding can offset a significant portion of the new service cost. In fact, with deliberate planning and system-wide optimization, curbside organics can serve not simply as an added service but as a catalyst for a more efficient, resilient, and sustainable solid waste system.

This analysis draws on eight established residential curbside organics programs and two active pilot programs representing communities of different sizes, densities, regions, service models, and participation structures. Across these communities, several findings emerge:

The community comparisons demonstrate the practical significance of these choices. In several communities that were studied, residents receive garbage, recycling, and organics collection at rates that are comparable to what residents in peer communities pay for garbage and recycling alone. For example, in Austin, Texas, residents pay approximately $29 per month for three-stream curbside service, compared with approximately $22 per month for garbage and recycling service in Raleigh, North Carolina. The comparison is not intended to suggest that every community can replicate a particular rate; rather, it demonstrates that the addition of organics does not necessarily translate into a proportionate increase in the total cost of residential solid waste service.

The Comparative Cost Analysis for Residential Curbside Organics Collection Programs report aims to support states and local communities in implementing effective strategies to fund residential curbside organic waste collection programs as a critical tool to improving resilience, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and diverting material from landfills and incinerators. The central implication for local governments is therefore straightforward: The affordability of curbside organics is largely a program design question. Communities considering organics collection can begin by evaluating the economics and performance of their existing solid waste system; identifying efficiencies that can help offset the new service; testing critical assumptions through a pilot, where appropriate; and finally, designing a full-scale program around the participation, collection, processing, and funding structures that best fit local conditions. To support this process, the report translates these findings into a three-phase implementation framework for evaluating the existing system, designing and testing an organics program, and moving toward financially sustainable full-scale implementation.

READ THE FULL REPORT: Comparative Cost Analysis for Residential Curbside Organics Collection Programs (PDF)

By Anya Obrez, Advocacy Associate, Food Waste, Nature, NRDC, and Darby Hoover, Senior Resource Specialist, Environmental Health & Nature, NRDC.

#5658. Who Can Weather the Health Storm?

States facing the greatest health damage from climate change are the least equipped to protect their residents.

Across the United States, climate change is intensifying extreme weather events, resulting in escalating public health harms and severe economic damage. For example, devastating inland flooding in Texas in 2025 killed 134 people and damaged $1 billion worth of residential property; 2025’s catastrophic wildfires in Southern California destroyed more than 10,000 buildings (at a cost of $63 billion) and triggered more than 8,000 health-care visits; and Hurricane Milton’s 2024 landfall in Florida killed 32 people and damaged $34 billion in property. These climate costs are typically borne by disaster victims, insurers, state agencies, and the federal government. Given the retreat of federal leadership from climate policy, state governments are increasingly looking to improve preparedness and resiliency in order to reduce future costs and health impacts.

However, a new analysis led by NRDC and published in the journal Health Affairs sheds light on key state-level gaps between climate change–linked health damage and levels of preparedness. We find that some of the most climate-burdened states are the least equipped to help their residents recover from climate disasters and prepare for future dangers. The intersection of escalating climate risks and adaptation vulnerabilities demands state policy intervention. Better integrating social protection policies into state climate resiliency plans can help states close these gaps and better safeguard their residents.

#5657. Diesel Prices Used To Be Cheaper Than Gas - Here's Why That Changed

Many Americans are not particularly happy about the country's soaring gas prices. Currently, the national average for diesel is $6.06 a gallon, and gasoline is at $3.87, according to AAA. While tensions in the Middle East have some part to play in increasing global crude oil prices, diesel being more expensive than gasoline is not something new in the country.

In fact, "On-highway diesel fuel prices have been higher than regular-grade gasoline prices, on a dollar-per-gallon basis, almost continuously since September 2004," according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA). Before that diesel was typically cheaper than gas, except during winter months when demand was high, as the fuel is commonly used in home heating.

Relatively high demand across Europe, China, India, and the United States is one of the reasons why diesel got more expensive than gasoline over the years. Beyond the usual supply-demand dynamics, other variables, like the push for low-sulfur diesels, also raised the fuel's production and distribution costs, due to the additional refining involved. Another contributing factor, per the EIA, is the federal excise tax for on-highway diesel, which is 6 cents a gallon higher than gasoline. Throw geopolitics and supply constraints into the mix, and you start to see why prices are so high.

The rate at which diesel prices rose when compared to AAA's data from the same time last year is quite staggering. While gasoline's national average was $3.08 a gallon, diesel's was at $3.76, meaning diesel jumped more than 60% during that period. And that's despite the U.S. running a diesel surplus and refineries churning out at near-maximum capacity with 97% utilization. So, why are diesel prices so high?

Despite less than 3% of U.S. passenger cars using diesel, the economy, whether it's shipping, logistics, agriculture, or construction, relies heavily on diesel. Compared to gasoline, diesel is a bit more inelastic, meaning price changes won't necessarily impact its demand. "People still drive a lot when gas prices go up, but consumers do vote with their pocketbook, and they will cut back on trips and stuff," says Gregg Ibendahl, an associate professor of agricultural economics at Kansas State University (via Scientific American). "When it comes to diesel fuel, though, it's not that way at all," Ibendahl continues, "Diesel price is $2.50 higher than what it was in spring, but that's not going to stop a single farmer from running their combine out there."

According to another EIA report, high crude oil prices and reduced refining activity in Russia, China, and the Middle East are part of the reason for the rising diesel prices in recent months. Ukraine targeted many of Russia's refineries, China suspended its fuel exports to protect its domestic stocks, and the Strait of Hormuz ... well, you know what's happening there. This naturally increases demand for exports from the United States, as the country is one of the largest producers of refined oil products in the world. If you weren't aware, the U.S. exports about 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day. Domestic consumption is around 3.6 million barrels per day, and the country refines roughly 5.3 million barrels per day, according to the American Action Forum. So, why not cut the exports like China did? Won't more domestic supply reduce diesel prices?

An export ban won't necessarily make things any better, reckons the aforementioned American Action Forum. According to its report, while an export ban may initially cool wholesale prices in the Gulf Coast (where major U.S. diesel production is concentrated), lower prices may not translate to other parts of the country because of logistics and infrastructure constraints.

In the case of New England, for example, it's much cheaper to import diesel from Canada than to source it domestically. The West Coast, Hawaii, and Alaska also import diesel to supplement their domestic supply. A sustained ban would eventually force U.S. refiners to cut back on production as they might face trouble finding options to absorb the excess supply. If refineries reduce production, it would drive up prices of all petroleum products, including diesel, which defeats the whole point of having the ban in the first place.

If global tensions continue and supply constraints remain, it's unlikely that diesel prices will come down. President Trump claiming "We don't need a deal with Iran" is certainly not a positive sign. Hopefully, the Democrats, now having won the midterms, could perhaps turn things around.

#5656. Trump Officials Will Fund New Research on Controversial Psychedelic Drug Ibogaine

— Veterans groups, psychedelic advocates say the drug has great promise for mental heath conditions

Federal officials on Thursday announced new funding to explore the medical potential of ibogaine, a controversial psychedelic drug championed by veterans, conservative lawmakers, and podcasters aligned with President Donald Trump.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said his department is awarding up to $4.9 million to prepare for the first U.S. studies of ibogaine for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), a hard-to-treat condition linked to higher suicide and substance abuse rates among veterans.

The money will not go directly to patient research, Kennedy said, but to lay the groundwork needed to manufacture, dose, and design studies of the drug.

Ibogaine is made from a shrub native to West Africa. It can cause intense hallucinations, nausea, vomiting, tremors, and sometimes deadly irregular heart rhythms. Ibogaine is currently illegal, in the same ultra-restrictive class as LSD, ecstasy, and most other psychedelic drugs.

Veterans organizations and psychedelic advocates contend that ibogaine has great promise for intractable conditions such as PTSD, severe depression, and opioid addiction. U.S. research on the drug has essentially been frozen for decades due to ibogaine's restricted status.

Kennedy said the government will receive data and treatment guidance from Beond Inc., a Texas-based company that has treated more than 3,000 patients with ibogaine in Mexico, where the drug is not illegal.

"That is going to allow us to dramatically accelerate the clinical trial process," Kennedy said. "We're going to have, I think, a record drug approval process."

Additional funding awards may explore ibogaine's use for addiction, he said.

Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins, who joined Kennedy for the announcement, said the collaborative effort would focus first on safety and "best-in-class research."

"For veterans living with PTSD, we owe them both urgency and the best science we can produce," Collins said.

Kennedy and Collins have previously voiced support for the potential of psychedelics, citing the experiences of veterans who have traveled abroad for therapy with ibogaine and other mind-altering substances.

Thursday's announcement was previewed in April, when Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to speed up review and research of psychedelics that could help with mental health conditions.

Three applications for psychedelics are pending review at the FDA. They include the first potential medicines made from psilocybin, the active ingredient in magic mushrooms, and MDMA, also called ecstasy. Decisions on those drugs could come within weeks or months.

Because of its safety risks, ibogaine research has moved more slowly.

The little data currently available mostly come from patients who have traveled to Mexico or other countries where ibogaine is not heavily regulated. Ibogaine clinics typically charge $10,000 to $20,000 for one course of treatment, which often involves monitoring of a patient's heart readings while emergency medical workers are on standby.

Trump's order on psychedelics came after podcaster Joe Rogan said he texted Trump about ibogaine, which he repeatedly has discussed on his show. According to Rogan, the president quickly responded: "Sounds great. Do you want FDA approval? Let's do it."

#5654. Is Using Launch Control Hard On Your Car, Especially If You Use It A Lot?

The sheer breadth of ability in modern performance cars is staggering. Take the seventh generation of the monstrous BMW M5. Critics love to point out that the plug-in hybrid super sedan is a bit porky, yet it still hits 60 mph in 3 seconds, pulls 0.98 g on the skidpad, and runs the quarter-mile in under 11 seconds in Car and Driver's testing. When it's done embarrassing sports cars, it'll carry five adults in comfort, and it's wrapped in more tech and safety kit than most of us will ever learn to use.

That kind of performance doesn't come down to silly power and no control. A big part of how heavy machines like the M5 get off the line so violently is launch control. In a combustion car, the system caps the revs while you hold the brake, then distributes power so the tires don't go up in smoke once you let go.

The idea behind launch control is to balance the power delivery with traction, so you can go as fast as possible without spinning the wheels. So, is launch control hard on your car? The short answer is that the system itself isn't.

Every full-throttle start puts a heavy load on the drivetrain, axles, and tires all at once. Do that over and over, and the clutch, transmission, and the rest of the drivetrain take the brunt of it. None of those parts are cheap, so if you've made a habit of launching at every green light, it's worth knowing what it's actually doing to your car.

Automakers are aware that repeated launches can be a problem, and that is why they advise you on how to use the feature. The BMW M4 owner's manual (available on ManualsLib) bluntly warns: "The use of Launch Control causes premature component wear." Kia's Stinger manual adds that leaning on it constantly "can put enormous stress on transmission, engine, and drive shafts." Both BMW and Kia also want owners to hold off until a new car's break-in period is done.

The Stinger disables launch control once its transmission fluid gets too hot, and BMW M won't allow repeated launches under certain conditions — you have to drive a bit for it to function again. Even the wait at the line is capped, with exhaust temperature restricting launch control to five seconds on the manual M3 and M4. Lexus caps how many times the LFA's launch control can be used, and the car's manual (hosted on ManualsLib) tells owners to "cruise at a normal speed for approximately 10 minutes" before launching again.

For the M3 and M4, though, BMW M says there's "no limitation of the launch control's availability over its lifetime." Porsche Livermore, a Porsche dealership, says launch control is "engineered for thrills, not daily commutes." The quickest factory cars that can hit 60 mph in 3 seconds or less usually rely on launch control to reach those silly numbers. Without it, acceleration can be noticeably slower. The Porsche 911 Carrera GTS T-Hybrid, for example, reached 60 mph in 2.5 seconds with launch control in Car and Driver's testing, compared with 3.1 seconds when accelerating from a 5-mph crawl.

Let's use a 2009 Nissan GT-R as an example. According to Cars.com, with stability control off and launch control on, one owner ended up with a $20,000 repair bill the warranty didn't cover. Though transmission failures were very rare, Nissan released new launch-control software that went easier on the transaxle.

At one point, a Nissan executive told Edmunds the 2009 GT-R would be the only one of its generation with launch control, but the 2010 car kept a reprogrammed version instead. Owners also sued, and the class-action case ended with 2009 cars getting new transmission software. By 2011, the GT-R launched at 3,300 rpm using controlled clutch slip, with stability control left on.

Things can go wrong in an instant, too. In 2018, a tuned GT-R that had been sitting cold at a car meet in Birmingham, England, lost its transmission on launch, all of it caught on video and reported by The Drive. Wheel hop is the violent shudder that occurs when a car launches with more power than its tires can handle, and it's a driveline killer. Dodge tackled it on the Challenger SRT Demon with a system called Launch Assist, which cuts the resulting driveline loads by up to 20%.

The Demon's follow-up, the Demon 170, claimed the quickest 0-to-60 time ever set by a production car, so you know the forces at play are serious. In most of these cases, something else stacked the odds against the car, whether it was a disabled safety net, a cold drivetrain, or a modified engine.

#5651. Why Some Traffic Lights Have A Yellow Border

If you're anything like me, in addition to scanning the road for distracted drivers and pedestrians, you also scan signs and roadsides for anything that could potentially be a red-light or speed camera. It feels like Big Brother is always watching and waiting for you to pass the 11 mph over-the-speed-limit threshold or to miss the "no right on red" sign nowadays, so there are a lot of things fighting for your attention when you're behind the wheel. If you've noticed that some traffic signals have a reflective yellow border while scanning your surroundings, you may wonder what they're for, but the simple fact that you've noticed them means they've served their purpose.

Those reflective yellow borders that surround some traffic signals have several intended purposes, including boosting signal visibility at night time, getting the attention of drivers with color vision deficiencies, and ensuring motorists are aware of an upcoming intersection, even when the lights are inoperative — in a power outage, for instance. The border is a simple and low-cost feature that has been proven to increase road safety.

A 2005 study titled "Safety Impact of Increased Traffic Signal Backboards Conspicuity" found that adding a three-inch yellow micro-prismatic retroreflective sheeting around the outer edge of a traffic signal backboard could reduce collisions by about 15%. The reflective material not only makes spotting traffic signals easier at night, but also in the daytime, particularly when signals are backlit at sunrise and sunset, as well as signals that are surrounded by reflective buildings and other visual distractions. The implementation of reflective yellow borders is not federally required at every intersection, so state and local transportation agencies usually decide where to install them.

The U.S. Department of Transportation's Federal Highway Administration considers adding a one-to-three-inch yellow retroreflective border to traffic signal backplates a "human factors enhancement of traffic signal visibility, conspicuity, and orientation." It cites the modification as a very low-cost, proven safety treatment, with the only potential concern being the integrity of the signal support structure in severe winds, which should be considered if adding a backplate to a signal in a wind-prone area.

#5650. The US Is Auctioning Seabed Near American Samoa. A $3 Million Bid Will Not Build a Mine.

On November 19, the US Marine Minerals Administration is scheduled to auction mineral rights covering about 31.5 million acres of seabed near American Samoa. The two areas have minimum bids of $3 million apiece, with 20-year lease terms. It is an impressive area and a modest opening price for a prospective new metals industry. The difference between the two numbers helps explain what the sale is actually offering.

The winning bidder will acquire a position from which to study mineral deposits and seek subsequent permissions. The government has said explicitly that an issued lease does not authorize commercial harvesting. It allows preliminary work such as mapping, while physical exploration, testing and mining require additional plans and approvals. The lease does not establish reserves, a collector that can work for years, a processing plant or buyers willing to pay enough for the metals.

The announcement is being treated as an American critical-minerals milestone. Investors should pay close attention to the difference between a government auction and an operating mining project. A mineral lease can have speculative value long before a profitable business exists.

In my new TFIE Strategy Briefing on the American Samoa auction, I examine how federal leasing can advance while the integrated business case remains weak.

The acreage has no direct relationship to the amount of commercially recoverable metal. The final federal notice describes northern and southern areas of roughly 16.3 million and 15.2 million acres. They are regulatory boundaries. A mining company needs deposit-grade and abundance data, continuity, recoverable tonnage, processing recoveries and a market price that leaves a margin after all the offshore and downstream costs.

The geology is becoming better understood. In April 2026, US Geological Survey scientists deployed 38 box cores in the Samoa Basin, of which 36 yielded enough material for nodule-density measurements. The expedition report is useful new evidence about the region. It is an expedition summary rather than a reserve statement for either lease area. Mineral distributions vary within the sampled region, and the better-studied Clarion-Clipperton Zone is not an adequate substitute for American Samoa’s own geological evidence.

Collection creates another set of costs. Impossible Metals proposes autonomous vehicles that select nodules and return to a support vessel. The Metals Company uses a more mature crawler-and-riser approach that has demonstrated recovery at pilot scale. Both must turn offshore demonstrations into dependable annual production, with maintenance, ship time, recovery systems and delays included. Their technologies should not be assigned the same engineering maturity, but neither has proved a profitable integrated mining-and-processing business.

In 2025, metallurgical engineer Lyle Trytten and I completed an independent techno-economic assessment commissioned by the National Ocean Protection Coalition. We examined both collection approaches, offshore operations, processing, metal markets and financial sensitivities. We judged commercial viability within the following 15 years highly unlikely. A new leasing process has not supplied the operating and financial evidence that was missing in that assessment.

The history of first-of-a-kind offshore production should influence the financing. Nautilus Minerals spent substantial capital on its Solwara-1 venture without reaching commercial production. Deep-sea mining depends on specialized machines, ships, handling systems, processing capacity and sales contracts working in sequence. The first production years of comparable projects are rarely smooth. The lease is one of the cheapest and earliest commitments in that chain.

American Samoa also has its own decision to make. Its government has supported scientific investigation while withholding support for commercial extraction at present. A lawsuit filed by Samoan chiefs and community groups contests the federal process. The resulting legal and territorial questions matter alongside engineering and economics. The environmental finding for preliminary leasing activities is not a finding about the effects of a future commercial mine.

Auction results will show what qualified bidders will pay for an opportunity. A winning bid can justify a company’s further studies and improve its fundraising story. An operating business will require years of capital investment, production evidence and profitable metal sales. Those are much harder milestones, and they remain ahead of the bidders.

Read A Seabed Lease Does Not Fix a Broken Business Case for the full assessment of the auction, and the Barnard–Trytten report for the underlying engineering and financial analysis.

#5649. How Much Power Would An EV's Solar Roof Provide?

When looking at modern EVs, it's all about efficiency. Manufacturers boast about impressive drag coefficient numbers, door handles that retract, large dish-style wheels, teardrop-shaped exterior design, as well as flat, covered underbodies. Furthermore, closed grilles, tapered rooflines, and active aerodynamic features that change the car's aero profile depending on usage are becoming increasingly common.

You could also point to cameras in place of side mirrors, low-rolling-resistance tires, and heat pumps that keep the cabin warm in winter without massively draining the battery. The list goes on. However, you might be wondering about solar roofs. By pure logic, an EV covered in solar panels would be more efficient overall, since every mile the sun puts back into the battery is a mile you don't have to plug in for. Or would it? Actual output naturally depends on sunlight, weather conditions, and location. We'll expand on why solar roofs aren't mainstream on EVs later, but for now, let's evaluate how much power an EV's solar roof could theoretically provide.

The Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems reports that its prototype solar roof's integrated photovoltaic cells produce approximately 19.5 watts per square foot under nominal conditions. On a 21.5-square-foot roof, by our math, that's roughly 420 watts of peak power. Fraunhofer says its roof could add approximately 6.2 miles of driving range per day in peak summer sun. Over a full year, Fraunhofer's figures for Freiburg, Germany, which assume no shade, point to about 10% more range.  Let's take a closer look at how much a solar roof can realistically do within the context of Los Angeles and a Tesla.

Picture a good old Tesla Model 3, one of the most popular EVs offering a leading range. Tesla doesn't list its roof area, so we'll stick with the 21.5-square-foot roof from earlier. Covered in cells rated at 19.5 watts per square foot, that roof would peak at 420 watts. Sunlight is measured in peak sun hours, the number of hours a day that add up to full-strength sun. Let's park it in sun-kissed Los Angeles, where data shows 5.62 peak sun hours a day as an average.

That gets our roof about 2.36 kWh (420 watts x 5.62 hours). In Edmunds' testing, the 2026 Model 3 Standard averaged 0.23 kWh per mile. Divide 2.36 by 0.23, and the roof adds about 10.3 miles a day (without energy losses), around 3% of the car's 321-mile EPA range. Summer's 6.14 hours bump that to about 11.2 miles, while winter's 5.03 drops it to 9.2. Again, those figures ignore the energy lost in charging, the added weight, aero penalties, etc.

Best case, that beats Fraunhofer's 6.2 miles, partly because the Model 3 uses 23 kWh per 100 miles versus Fraunhofer's assumed 27.4. And, for fun, how many Harbor Freight panels for 30 miles a day? That takes 6.9 kWh, or seven Predator 200-watt foldables in LA ($1,609.93 at the time of writing). That's 1,400 watts, more than triple the roof. Using 10-watt Thunderbolt trickle chargers, it's 123, for $5,533.77, plus a power station or inverter to feed the car. Ultimately, even in the best possible scenario, you still need to keep your charging cable handy.

EVs haven't jumped on the solar roof bandwagon for a few reasons. To start, there really isn't much roof to work with (as our Harbor Freight examples showed). A car roof is a small surface, and a panel only hits its rated output in full, direct sunlight. Overcast skies, winter's shorter days, and a layer of road dust all chip away at what the panels make, and a car that regularly parks in a garage collects next to nothing. The aforementioned Fraunhofer estimate is very optimistic, since it assumes a sunny, unshaded day. Solar Team Eindhoven's Stella Terra, a lightweight, student-built off-roader with a smaller battery, drove across Morocco to the Sahara, covering 621 miles without plugging into a charger. Now picture it in Seattle in January.

Then you have the added weight and complexity that comes with these panels. This can work against the efficiency promise, since added weight means the car burns more energy to get moving. Additionally, unless the panels are built flush into the roof, they become one more thing for air to trip over, undermining aero efficiency. These obstacles don't mean solar can't provide supplemental range, but the application isn't as practical as some might perceive it to be.

#5648. Prescriptions Down 25%, Overdoses Cut in Half: What Stopped a Gabapentinoid Surge?

— Study identifies three interventions that may have influenced pregabalin use

High-profile media coverage of the harms associated with the gabapentinoid pregabalin (Lyrica) and tighter safeguards coincided with fewer prescriptions and overdoses in Australia, a retrospective study showed.

Following a media campaign, tighter dispensing rules, and boxed warnings, pregabalin prescriptions and overdoses dropped significantly below projected trends -- falling by 25% and 47%, respectively -- reported Rose Cairns, PhD, of the University of Sydney, and co-authors in The BMJ.

This was a reversal from a steep upward trajectory that had persisted since 2013, the researchers noted. The shift corresponded to ongoing monthly reductions in prescriptions of 0.7% (95% CI 0.5-0.9) and in poison center overdose calls of 1.6% (95% 1.0-2.3).

Australia historically has had a big problem with pregabalin use and overdose, and many other countries face similar issues, Cairns noted.

"Importantly, the interventions that were associated with a decrease in harms included things like raising public awareness of the risks via the media and boxed warnings. These relatively 'soft' interventions can still have an impact," she told MedPage Today.

The findings are "really positive, but we think use of pregabalin is still far too high," Cairns continued. "There's a lot of off-label use for conditions with minimal evidence to back that up. And while high-risk use has decreased, we really need to continue to minimize co-use with opioids, which has been shown to increase the risk of death."

Gabapentinoids -- pregabalin and gabapentin -- were originally developed as antiseizure drugs. Subsequent indications have expanded to include neuropathic pain, postherpetic neuralgia, and fibromyalgia.

"Despite this relatively narrow range of approved indications, gabapentinoids are considered 'blockbuster' drugs," Cairns and colleagues wrote. "High-income countries have the highest rates of gabapentinoid consumption, while low- and middle-income countries have had the highest consumption growth in recent years. Most of this consumption is driven by off-label use for non-registered indications."

In the U.S., pregabalin is scheduled under the Controlled Substances Act. Gabapentin is not scheduled at the federal level but eight states have enacted legislation to classify gabapentin as a schedule V controlled substance.

In 2019, the FDA warned that respiratory depression or death may occur in patients taking pregabalin or gabapentin with opioid pain medicines or other drugs that depress the central nervous system. Despite this, co-prescribing of gabapentinoids and opioids persists.

In the U.K., one-third of substance use deaths involve a gabapentinoid, predominantly pregabalin, and deaths involving gabapentinoids have more than doubled from 2018 to 2022, Cairns and co-authors noted.

The study in Australia is "timely and rigorous, but these figures warrant caution," noted David Juurlink, MD, PhD, of the Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre in Toronto, in an accompanying editorial. "The ecological design cannot establish causation, and poison center calls are an imperfect measure of poisoning incidence, influenced by reporting practices and patterns of healthcare use," he pointed out.

Pregabalin should be used more selectively, Juurlink argued. "Although it can provide meaningful relief in some patients with neuropathic pain or fibromyalgia, most do not achieve substantial pain relief," he wrote.

"For other painful conditions, the evidence is even less encouraging," Juurlink added. "Randomized trials and meta-analyses have found no convincing evidence of benefit for low back pain or sciatica, conditions for which the drug is nevertheless frequently prescribed. Pregabalin's commercial success, in other words, has far outstripped its demonstrated clinical utility."

To evaluate pregabalin use and misuse in Australia, Cairns and colleagues evaluated dispensing claims and poison center overdose data from 2016 to 2024, focusing on three key events: widespread media reporting about the harms of pregabalin in December 2018, tighter prescribing restrictions after April 2020, and the introduction of boxed warnings in February 2021.

The researchers randomly sampled 10% of Australians with drug subsidies and 50% of calls placed to the country's largest poison control center. During the study period, 227,864 people were dispensed 3,441,851 pregabalin prescriptions, and 4,871 pregabalin overdose calls were reported.

Use and overdoses peaked in 2018 before plateauing and declining. Dispensing dropped significantly at three time points: in December 2018 (corresponding to high-profile press coverage), in May 2020 (after tighter prescribing restrictions were introduced), and in December 2021 (after boxed warnings were in effect).

The findings are observational, the researchers acknowledged. The study analyzed subsidized prescriptions only and poisons center data may be subject to reporting bias, they added. The researchers also could not determine patients' access to pain treatments.

#5647. Zoox Launches Robotaxis in Atlanta

The year of the robotaxi rolls on. Just after writing about Zoox expanding its robotaxi service in Las Vegas, I see news that Zoox is entering Atlanta!

“Our initial rollout will focus on the Northwest region of Atlanta, near Atlantic Station, Woodward, and Home Park. We will expand throughout the year as our testing progresses,” Zoox shares.

To start with, in order to work out any bugs and avoid controversy, the service can only be used by Zoox employees, family members, and friends. But that should change fairly soon. “We look forward to opening our waitlist for Atlanta in the coming months, ahead of the launch of our Zoox Explorers early rider program.”

I do find it interesting that Zoox, Waymo, and Tesla are all in a sort of fast (but sort of small) expansion phase at the same time. They each keep adding more cities, but with quite limited geographic ranges and vehicle fleets. Is it all the early budding of robotaxi services that will bloom into giant networks? Or is it companies rushing to try to prove their viability and build up economies of scale, but which might not actually be financially viable and profitable in the long run — or even next year? We’ll have to wait to see. In the meantime, it’s certainly exciting each time a new area is opened up and more electric robotaxis hit the road.

In case you have forgotten where Zoox is in operation, the company informs us: “Atlanta marks our newest testing market for the robotaxi. This is in addition to testing in Austin and Miami, our public service in Las Vegas, and our Zoox Explorers early rider program in San Francisco.”

Also of note is the fact that Zoox didn’t just decide last month to go to Atlanta and rush into the market. It has been laying the groundwork for this launch for about a year and a half in the city. “We started operations in Atlanta in the Spring of 2025, using our testing fleet to map and learn about local driving behaviors, weather patterns, and the city infrastructure. Since then, we have been steadily expanding our driving capabilities, including beginning autonomous driving, and growing our geofence, fleet size, and team to prepare for this next stage of testing.” Zoox explains further how this is central to how Zoox operates:

“Zoox has always been thoughtful and measured in our approach to rolling out autonomous technology at every level. Before we even hit the road and begin driving with our testing fleet in any capacity, we first engage with local and state officials and regulators. Our philosophy is ‘no surprises’ as we lay the foundations for future service markets.

“Along with engaging with local and state officials and regulators, we also love partnering with the community. Workforce development starts long before a first job. That’s why we’re partnering with @Promise Center to help local youth learn, grow, and prepare for their futures in a safe, supportive environment. This partnership reflects our commitment to the Atlanta community. We’re excited to continue investing in the next generation and the future of this city.”

Circling back to Atlanta and why the company has made that one of the first cities for its robotaxi deployment, Zoox adds the following: “Atlanta is a dynamic, vibrant city. Known as the ‘Silicon Valley of the South,’ it boasts one of the largest ride-hailing markets in the United States. Atlanta’s dense, urban layout creates strong demand for efficient transportation solutions, which is where on-demand autonomous ride-hailing comes in. It also has a growing population, and demand like this is exactly why we’re excited to bring Zoox to Atlantans.”

Lastly, as I also highlighted in my article last night about Zoox expanding in Las Vegas, one key thing Zoox is proud of and argues sets it apart from the competition is how vertically integrated its robotaxi business is and how useful the design of its vehicle is for its purpose. Here’s more: “While Atlanta has become a hub for autonomous testing, Zoox continues to stand apart from other companies. Unlike the retrofitted solutions currently on the road, our robotaxi was built from the ground up for fully autonomous ride-hailing. It has no steering wheel or driver’s seat, instead featuring spacious, carriage-style seating for up to four passengers. This design layout allows us to offer Zoox passengers more than just a ride; we are providing a private space where riders can socialize, relax, and reclaim their time. […]

“Zoox owns, operates, and assembles its vehicles, and is the only company currently deploying a fully driverless, purpose-built robotaxi on public roads in the U.S.

“We see promise in bringing our robotaxi service to Atlanta, and look forward to offering Atlantans this unique and private space to socialize, rock out, and create their own experience while being transported to their destination.”

You can learn more on the Zoox website or the Zoox app.

#5646. Waymo Encounters Police Blockade And Speeds Right By, Because Of Course It Did

As far as robotaxis go, Waymos are supposed to be about as good as it gets. No one at Waymo is talking about selling these vehicles to the general public, they're covered in arrays of advanced sensors that Teslas don't even bother trying to match, and plenty of people who have ridden in them got where they were going without any issues. Even Waymos still have problems, though. Like one of their cars apparently speeding past the police blockade you'll see in the video below.

A viewer identified as @luluesque allowed ABC7 News to use the video they captured of what appears to be a pass that would immediately lead to a human driver being pulled over and ticketed. Two police cars are weaving to slow down highway traffic, performing what's known as a "traffic break," a pretty common situation in California — in this case, because there's a construction vehicle ahead, with workers standing in the freeway. The Waymo attempts to speed past in the left lane, before the police cars maneuver themselves to block it from getting by.

Of course, since the Waymo in question was a robotaxi, there was no driver to cite. You also don't have to be a traffic nerd to understand why it's so dangerous for robotaxis to still need more training when it comes to safely and legally operating around emergency vehicles.

In Waymo's defense, there's no way its robotaxis could be more dangerous that Teslas running a glorified version of the same so-called "Full Self-Driving" software that recent testing found loved to speed, illegally pass cyclists, and ignore various other traffic laws. Much like impressing a woman romantically, the bar for beating Tesla on safety is in hell, and we would all expect Waymo to clear it with minimal effort. "Significantly safer than Tesla" means about as much as "way safer than juggling kitchen knives."

Waymo's robotaxis don't exactly have a spotless record either. From things like getting stuck in a three-way standoff to honking all night, dooring a cyclist into another Waymo, hitting a child that darted out in front of one, recently having to pause highway operations, and more, Waymo's robotaxis have made more than their fair share of mistakes along the way. And with so many of them clogging up the roads in cities all across the country, it's always important to remember they're still imperfect. I'd still ride in a Waymo 10 times before I'd ride in a Tesla robotaxi once, but even Waymos still have issues.

#5645. Study Pinpoints States with Steepest Warming Trends Since 1980

The findings indicate where adaptive measures are needed most around the United States.

Global warming, the observed increase in the Earth’s average global surface temperature since preindustrial (1850-1900) times, currently stands at around 1.63 degrees Celsius. While this number is expected to continue to rise, local temperatures will not go up uniformly around the world. In regions where warming trends are most pronounced, local adaptation and resilience measures will be especially critical to minimizing risks to ecosystems, agricultural productivity, the built environment, human health, and economic well-being.

To that end, a new open-access study in the journal Scientific Data identifies the highest-risk regions for warming within the United States. Using data from well-known, high-resolution climate and weather datasets (MERRA2 and ERA5) covering the years 1980-2022, researchers at the MIT Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy (CS3) report global warming-attributed trends in monthly-averaged maximum daily temperature for every U.S. state.

The study finds that Alaska, Utah, New Mexico, Colorado, and Nevada have experienced the strongest average warming trends; the lowest occurred in Hawaii, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Arkansas. Across the country, warming trends were most pronounced during the summer and fall, particularly in September and November. Alaska has the highest historical maximum daily temperature warming (an average of 2.5 C of monthly-averaged maximum daily temperature increase per degree of global warming), while Hawaii has the lowest average historical warming, at 0.8 C.

The authors expect that barring unforeseen local anomalies, these state-by-state temperature trends will continue unabated as ongoing global emissions from human activities continue to raise the average global temperature.

“Based on these results, we encourage decision-makers to assess states that have undergone the steepest increases in maximum and minimum daily temperatures, and identify where continued trends would indicate a rapid progression toward thresholds beyond which natural and managed resources, ecosystems, and infrastructure can function safely,” says MIT CS3 Deputy Director C. Adam Schlosser, a co-author of the study. “In such cases, triaging and adaptive measures would take a high priority. By directing resources to where they are needed most, state and regional planners could significantly reduce climate-related physical and financial risks.”

Unlike previous efforts to report temperature trends across the United States, this study aggregates average maximum, minimum, and mean daily temperature data at the state level for each month of the year, providing actionable information for planners in government, industry, and civil society.

By Mark Dwortzan | Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy, MIT

#5644. Major Change to Prostate Cancer Screening Guidelines

— ACS now recommends PSA testing every 2 years for average-risk men ages 50 to 69

Shifting gears on prostate cancer screening, the American Cancer Society (ACS) now recommends screening with prostate-specific antigen (PSA) every 2 years for average-risk men ages 50 to 69.

Since the release of its previous guideline 16 years ago, the ACS had recommended that average-risk men consult with a physician before deciding for themselves whether to undergo a screening PSA test.

The new ACS recommendations also strengthened guidelines for men at high risk for prostate cancer, recommending annual screening beginning at age 45 for Black men and those with a strong family history of the disease. The organization previously recommended that those men discuss the pros and cons of screening with a physician at age 40 or 45.

The changes reflect the accumulation of stronger evidence that screening PSA tests reduce prostate cancer mortality and diagnosis of late-stage disease, according to the updated guidelines from Robert Smith, PhD, ACS senior vice president for early cancer detection science, and colleagues, appearing in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians.

"We've just reached a point in our understanding of prostate cancer, especially that [screening] can reduce the risk of being diagnosed with metastatic disease and dying of prostate cancer," Smith told MedPage Today. "We have good protocols for avoiding harms."

Smith noted that the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) has not updated their prostate cancer screening guidelines since 2018. For average-risk men, the USPSTF recommends discussion-backed decisions on PSA testing for men ages 55 to 69.

"I cannot tell you what [their recommendations] would be if they updated them today, but they did not have the data in 2018 that we had in 2025 with the update of the European trial data showing the endurance of the mortality reduction," said Smith.

The update aligns with recent evidence supporting PSA screening for prostate cancer as "one of the most important steps men can take to protect their health," said Ash Tewari, MD, of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City.

"We have strong evidence that PSA testing can reduce the risk of dying from prostate cancer, and advances in MRI and other diagnostic tools are helping us identify potentially dangerous cancers while avoiding unnecessary procedures," he said. "Knowing your risk, getting screened regularly, and having these conversations early can save lives."

With the update, the ACS takes a clear position on prostate cancer screening, said Mark Ashamalla, MD, of Episcopal Health Services in New York City.

"For years, the ACS largely focused on encouraging men to discuss the pros and cons of PSA screening with their doctors," said Ashamalla. "Now they're taking a much clearer position and actually recommending regular screening. For men at average risk, that means a PSA blood test every 2 years between ages 50 and 69, while Black men and those with a strong family history should begin annual screening at age 45. This is a significant shift and reflects growing evidence that regular screening can reduce the risk of advanced prostate cancer and save lives."

"The goal isn't to find and treat every prostate cancer," he added. "It's to catch the dangerous ones early enough to make a difference. I think that's the biggest takeaway from these new guidelines."

By way of the guidelines, the ACS also recommends:

The updated guidelines are supportive of the recent trend toward active surveillance as the primary option for men with low-risk prostate cancer.

"It's important to recognize that prostate cancer screening has evolved over the past 30 years," said Smith. "More and more people appreciate that very worrisome harms associated with therapy can be avoided, especially if a man is diagnosed with prostate cancer that is not aggressive. Active treatment should be avoided until such time as it appears that the disease has become aggressive. Some men may be diagnosed with a prostate cancer that's not very aggressive, and they will live with it in that state for the rest of their lives. [They can] avoid harms that are quite diminishing to quality of life."

"On the other hand, if a man's prostate cancer becomes more aggressive, and treatment is necessary, then the process of active surveillance will at least have postponed it for a number of years, allowing men to not have to live with those [treatment-related] side effects," said Smith.

#5643. AI Businesses Still Bleeding Billions

AI is fun and cool when it creates useful things for you or answers tough questions quickly and well (let’s not focus on AI slop and false claims at the moment), but that doesn’t mean AI businesses are financially sustainable or sensible. AI companies are still heavily subsidizing their broad use, with the benefits for them being growing user bases and sky-high valuations. These companies are burning billions of dollars each quarter on the hype and promise that they will rule the world one day (quite literally).

OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, reported this week that it had $10.9 billion in operating losses last quarter. That’s up from $10.1 billion in operating losses in the second quarter.

One might think that means not a lot changed, and certainly nothing positive. However, the company’s revenue was actually up by 50%! So, even with a huge boost in revenue, gigantic losses grew! Furthermore, the company was apparently even using a tool of “last resort” here.

OpenAI started running ads in ChatGPT, something that the company was adamantly trying to avoid. CEO Sam Altman previously called the proposal to run ads “unsettling” and claimed that the company would only go that route as a matter of “last resort.” Well, it seems the company has reached that point of last resort. And that can’t be a good thing, right? Considering that OpenAI is still losing billions of dollars a quarter, it’s even more concerning. What comes after a “last resort” effort to turn finances around?

Frankly, I wish we could spend billions of dollars a quarter to make CleanTechnica into a behemoth of a media organization! That would be amazing — imagine all of the stuff we could do! But what are the chances we’d be losing billions of dollars a quarter in doing so? And how long could we operate like that before external sources of funding stopped covering the bill?

As we know, OpenAI is one of the “leaders” of the AI industry. If it is struggling like this, who isn’t, and what does that mean for the industry overall and where it’s headed?

The one big player that has been raking in the dough in the midst of this enormous AI craze is NVIDIA, and look at what’s now happening there! Where are things going to go with that company?

“The news comes not long after controversy over how OpenAI was projecting its earnings. In October, the company reported an annualized revenue, an estimate of how much money it will earn over a year, of about $50 billion — which was $20 billion short of what it told investors only a month before,” Futurism adds. “The discrepancy was taken as an admission that the business models of AI companies weren’t as robust as their leadership was making them out to be, fueling speculation of an impending bubble.”

Why can’t the leaders of these companies just ask their chatbots how to turn a profit and implement their answers? Well, one of the answers might have been regulatory capture and blocking others from entering the market, but that dream may now be out the window. In my humble opinion, 2027 could be a very interesting year for AI companies, and that might involve a big popping noise.

#5642. Why Some Cars Will Have More Physical Buttons In The Near Future

Physical buttons could officially make a comeback, and the reasons are straightforward: Drivers pushed back, safety testers sided with them, and even China has proposed making physical controls mandatory for critical functions. After a decade of hybridization, electrification, and shifting buyer tastes, it turns out that more tech doesn't automatically mean a better car.

Last year, we looked at how some car brands are rethinking touchscreens and bringing back physical buttons, and that's no longer a vague promise. It's happening in real cars right now. Ferrari is a good example. Customers criticized the touch controls on the SF90's steering wheel, so Ferrari reworked the design, and the 2027 Amalfi has real buttons. Ferrari is also offering a retrofit to owners stuck with the touch controls, and the Purosangue, the 12Cilindri, and the Roma are among the cars covered.

It isn't just about luxury cars, either. Volkswagen's ID.Tiguan, the ID.4's replacement, arrives in Europe in early 2027 with physical buttons in the cabin, and the Golf GTI and Cupra Born now use physical switches on their steering wheels. Mercedes is doing it, too, on the electric GLC's new steering wheel, and so is Audi with its upcoming A4 E-tron and Q7 E-tron.

So the industry is clearly leaning back toward the tactile. However, its previous move away from buttons isn't easy to undo, so the answer takes more than flipping a switch. It takes a closer look at what drivers actually want and what carmakers can realistically build.

Only partly. The Drive reported that 48% of shoppers in an AutoPacific survey picked dials or buttons over a screen. That's nearly half, yet 60% of respondents also said they like how screens look. Drivers aren't asking for a 1990s dashboard. They want a better balance. As Kelley Blue Book reported, Telemetry's Sam Abuelsamid says physical controls take "a lot of engineering effort," which is why the brands above are keeping screens but bringing buttons back where it counts.

Modern cars pack in a ton of features, and if every one of them got its own button, a luxury interior could start to look like a 747 cockpit. Regulations play a part, too. Since May 2018, new U.S. vehicles under 10,000 pounds have been required to have a backup camera, which puts a screen in the dashboard of nearly every new car. Once there, it makes a convenient home for everything else.

It's not just automakers that are scrutinizing the all-touchscreen dashboard. China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has proposed rules that would require physical controls for critical functions in new models starting in 2027. Europe's independent safety testers are pushing in a similar direction. Euro NCAP's 2026 test results came with a headline that says it all: "Buttons are back for basic functions."

Even Jony Ive, designer of the iPhone and the Ferrari Luce, says touchscreens are not the way to go for the future. So it's reasonable to expect a middle ground: screens for the extras, and real buttons for anything you shouldn't have to take your eyes off the road to use.

Increasingly, yes, and some carmakers are really going for it. The BMW Neue Klasse iX3 debuts a voice assistant powered by Amazon's Alexa+, the same kind of large-language tech behind today's AI chatbots. And TechCrunch reports that Rivian's software chief, Wassym Bensaid, believes in-car buttons are an "anomaly," and a car is "a fantastic environment for AI." Hey, even Mercedes believes you should be able to have a natural conversation with your car.

The logic behind the claim is sound. If a car can understand what you mean, nobody should have to hunt through a menu for the defroster. We've already established that cars have too many functions today for them to be translated into buttons. Voice can be a lot quicker. Telling a car to play something on Spotify takes less time and attention than going into the menus, typing in the song, finding it, and hitting play. From a safety perspective, voice commands can reduce the time drivers spend looking away from the road, although they won't eliminate distraction altogether.

The same goes for changing radio stations, entering navigation directions, and plenty of other things. Automotive technology is advancing rapidly, and manufacturers like Volkswagen are already building ChatGPT into their voice assistants. Although AI still isn't able to take control directly, it does feel like a natural next step.

#5640. Fabric Molds Could Bring Material-Saving Concrete Beams Within Reach

MIT engineers cast a concrete beam using a sewn fabric mold with one-third the amount of concrete and half as much steel as a conventional beam.

Topology optimization is a computer design method that can help engineers design beams using reduced amounts of concrete and steel. But those intricate shapes produced from the tool are often too complex or expensive to pour into conventional rigid molds. The few that have been built have mostly relied on specialized equipment, such as concrete 3D printers or machine-carved molds, equipment that is out of reach in regions where new construction is expected to grow.

Now, MIT engineers have shown that highly efficient beams can be cast in something more accessible: sewn fabric. In a paper published in the Journal of Building Engineering, the team designed and built a 3-meter (about 10-foot) test beam using fabric molds created through an automated pattern-making process. Compared with a conventional beam designed to carry the same weight, the optimized beam used about one-third as much concrete and half as much steel reinforcement. When tested, its measured response was within about 2 percent of what the team’s computer model predicted.

Fabric formwork, in which concrete is poured into a mold made of textile, has been explored for years to create beams that vary in depth, rather than in rectangular shapes common in construction. But because fabric deforms under the weight of wet concrete, that flexibility has made the final shape hard to predict.

“The key realization was that this flexibility is not just a limitation to manage; with the right computational pattern design, it can become a way to produce optimized structural forms,” says Josephine Carstensen, the Gilbert W. Winslow (1937) Career Development Professor in Civil Engineering and senior author of the study.

Fabric molds can also be inexpensive, lightweight, and fast compared to wood or steel molds. “You could sew a formwork together off site, pack it into a box, and bring it to a job site very easily,” says Jackson Jewett PhD ’25, co-author of the study. “We joke that we are developing the H&M of the construction industry.”

Cement production accounts for roughly 8 percent of human-caused carbon emissions.

“This work addresses concrete’s climate footprint primarily by reducing material demand,” Carstensen says. “Cement production is highly carbon-intensive, so using less concrete is an important part of decarbonizing construction.”

Where new construction happens matters, too. The world’s number of buildings is expected to nearly double by 2050, with about 85 percent of that growth in developing countries, where access to advanced construction equipment is often limited. That is why, Carstensen says, the team focused on an accessible, cost-conscious fabrication approach.

Concrete is strong when compressed, but weak when pulled, so it’s reinforced with steel that can handle the pulling forces. The researchers first mapped a path for the steel reinforcement using a method called graphic statics, which can generate structural designs almost instantly. They used it to shape the steel bar so that it carries an equal share of the weight along its entire length to keep the reinforcement simple enough for builders to make. Topology optimization, which works more slowly but can place material freely, was used to determine where concrete was needed and where material could be removed from areas where it contributes little to the structural performance.

“Both methods are good at different things, so we tried to combine the strengths of both into a single methodology,” says Jewett.

The resulting beam has a top section, narrow angled legs, and a thin bottom section for the steel reinforcement. The team’s automated process translated the 3D beam design into flat fabric pieces that can be cut and sewn into a mold, accounting for how the fabric will deform once concrete is poured in. A simple timber frame supported the finished fabric mold.

For Mark Hellrich SM ’26, the study’s lead author, the main hands-on challenge was getting the concrete mix right. Woven cotton fabric lets water seep through, so a mix that is too runny loses water through the mold. It also presses harder against the fabric, pushing it away from the intended shape.

The team used a moderately wet, sand-rich mix with only small stones, so the concrete could flow through the beam’s narrow, angled legs and thin bottom section without getting stuck. They then packed it in by hand, prodding each layer and tapping and kneading the fabric from the outside.

“This is where the flexibility of the mold becomes an advantage: you can work the concrete through the interconnected passages without a vibrator, which a rigid mold of this shape would need,” says Hellrich. A concrete vibrator is a tool typically used to shake air pockets out of freshly poured concrete in rigid molds.

Once the concrete was in place, the wet fabric revealed the beam’s final shape. “All three beams were free of wrinkles and creases,” says Hellrich. The top surface stayed close to the design, while the main difference was a downward sag along the bottom, with the angled legs folding slightly inward.

To find out how much sewing precision the beam needs, the team built three molds for the same design, made from 36, 56, and 76 fabric pieces. Comparing the 3D scans of the cast beams with the target design, the researchers found that more seams gave finer control over the details, but did not necessarily make the beam’s overall shape more accurate.

“More seams improve local control because they divide the fabric into smaller, more constrained panels. But a more complex pattern also has more pieces to align and more seam length, so small cutting, sewing, and assembly inaccuracies can accumulate across the mold, explains Carstensen.

The 56-piece mold demonstrated the best balance, capturing the important design geometry without the added time, effort, and potential errors associated with the most complex pattern.

The researchers then load-tested one of the beams, gradually stacking 36 water-filled buckets on top of it, up to about 30 percent of its design load to reflect everyday service conditions. Weighted lines hung from the beam’s underside to precise measuring gauges below, tracking how far the beam bent as the load was added and removed. At the beam’s center, the measured deflection — its downward movement under the load — was within about 2 percent of the computer model’s prediction.

The team also compared the cost of a single fabric-formed beam with a conventional one and found that location makes all the difference. In the Global South, where materials tend to cost more relative to labor, all three fabric versions were cheaper, with savings of about 10 to 20 percent. In the Global North, higher labor costs for sewing reversed that advantage, making the fabric versions about 16 to 55 percent more expensive.

The findings suggest that fabric formwork is most promising for custom-shaped concrete components produced as a one-off or in small batches, such as exposed beams, roof or long-span framing, pedestrian structures, and landscape elements. For the repetitive, rectangular beams found in most buildings, conventional reusable molds remain the more economical choice where labor is expensive.

“To get started, a builder would need the digital pattern for the target component, a sewing machine and suitable fabric, and a simple timber support frame,” Carstensen says. “That is a much lower equipment threshold than robotic fabrication, concrete 3D printing, or CNC-milled molds.”

The researchers describe the 3-meter beam as a proof of concept comparable to a short building span. It is also a big step up from the 1.2-meter beam the team built in a previous project, Jewett notes.

Building bigger isn’t just a matter of enlarging the design, Carstensen notes. As a beam gets longer, its own weight and the pressure on the fabric mold change, so a larger beam would need a new design. The next step, Carstensen says, is “to test multiple beams to failure.”

“The nice thing about these optimization methods is they generate structures that look organic,” Jewett says. “Their geometries are clear expressions of how the forces move through the structural system. There is elegance to them. It makes you ask why we don’t design all our structures in this way.”

Joining Carstensen, Jewett, and Hellrich on the paper are co-authors Abhinit Sati, Edward Chien, and Emily Whiting, of Boston University’s Department of Computer Science.

The work was partially supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation.
